practice_questions.text: Give two names used for God in Hinduism.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two of: Brahman; Brahma; Vishnu; Shiva; Krishna; Rama; Ganesh; Hanuman. 'Atman' is not a name for God: it is the individual soul.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by 'atman' in Hinduism?
practice_questions.marks: Two marks for: the individual soul or true self within each living being, believed to be eternal and indestructible. One mark for a partial answer: 'the soul' or 'the self'.

practice_questions.text: Describe Hindu beliefs about the nature of Brahman.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Detailed description covering Brahman as ultimate reality and universal soul, source of all life (Chandogya Upanishad 3:14.1), present in all things (Katha Upanishad 5:2), the salt-in-water analogy, and the relationship with atman. Includes explanation of why this matters (all life has divine value). Secure: Clear description of Brahman as ultimate reality, with reference to sacred text and the one-and-many nature. Developing: Basic description of Brahman as 'God' or 'the universal soul' without development. Emerging: Simple statement that Brahman is God.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the concept of avatar influences the way Vaishnavas practise their faith.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains what an avatar is (Vishnu's descent to earth in physical form), cites Bhagavad Gita 4:5-8 (Krishna appears when righteousness declines), identifies key avatars (Krishna, Rama), explains influence: devotion to Krishna through bhakti and Hare Krishna chant; celebrating festivals such as Diwali (Rama's return); reading the Bhagavad Gita as Krishna's direct teaching; pilgrimage to sites associated with Krishna. Secure: Clear explanation of avatar concept with two developed examples of influence. Developing: Basic explanation of avatars; limited influence points. Emerging: Names Krishna or Rama without connecting to the avatar concept.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Hindu beliefs about the relationship between Brahman and atman.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Belief 1: Brahman pervades all living beings including the individual atman — the Katha Upanishad (5:2) teaches Brahman dwells within the hearts of all. Belief 2: The atman is eternal and indestructible while the body is mortal — Bhagavad Gita 2:17 states the soul cannot be destroyed. Could also reference Advaita Vedanta teaching that atman and Brahman are ultimately one. Secure: Two beliefs explained with at least one textual reference; some development. Developing: Two beliefs stated; one or both underdeveloped or lacking a source. Emerging: One belief with little development.

practice_questions.text:
'It is impossible to worship just one God if you believe in the Hindu Trimurti.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument. Agrees: The Trimurti presents three distinct divine figures with different functions; popular Hinduism includes many deities; Vaishnavism and Shaivism offer different supreme deities. Disagrees: The Trimurti is understood as three aspects of the one Brahman; all deities are ultimately manifestations of the single divine reality; the Bhagavad Gita (7:21) teaches that all devotion ultimately reaches the one God. Non-religious view: a Humanist might argue the multiplicity of deities reflects evolving human attempts to conceptualise the divine rather than evidence of actual theological contradiction. Justified conclusion. Secure: Two developed sides with at least one Hindu source; some evaluation. Developing: Some points on both sides, limited evaluation. Emerging: Descriptive, one-sided.

practice_questions.text: Give two attributes Christians use to describe God.
practice_questions.marks: Award one mark for each of two correct attributes from: omnipotence / omnibenevolence / omniscience / omnipresence / creator / sustainer. Accept brief descriptions if clearly referring to the correct attribute.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'omnipotence'?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Precise definition — God is all-powerful, able to do anything that is not logically self-contradictory. Secure: God is all-powerful / nothing is impossible for God. Developing: Vague — 'God is very powerful' without specifying 'all-powerful'. Emerging: No clear definition.

practice_questions.text: Describe Christian beliefs about God as creator and sustainer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Accurate description with developed explanation of ex nihilo creation from Genesis 1:1-3, the meaning of sustainer (God maintains existence), and why both matter for Christian belief. Secure: Describes creation from nothing and sustaining role with some use of Genesis. Developing: General points about God making the world; limited use of sources. Emerging: Simple statement — 'God made everything' — with little or no development.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the parable of the prodigal son (Luke 15:11-32) helps Christians understand the nature of God the Father.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains the father's unconditional welcome of the son before apology; links to omnibenevolence; explains what this teaches about God's forgiveness being freely available; may contrast with the older brother's resentment as a foil to divine love. Secure: Correct plot reference; clear link to God's love and forgiveness. Developing: Plot summary with limited theological connection. Emerging: Vague reference to the parable without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Bible provides evidence for the Christian belief in the Trinity.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two distinct biblical passages (e.g. John 1:1-3 for the Son as eternal Word; Galatians 5:22-23 for the Spirit's transforming work), each explained in detail with a clear link to Trinitarian doctrine. No confusion between the three persons. Secure: Two passages identified and correctly linked to the Father, Son or Spirit with clear explanation. Developing: One passage explained well; the second underdeveloped or confused. Emerging: Vague reference to 'the Bible teaches the Trinity' without specific texts.

practice_questions.text: 'Christians cannot make sense of God as both one and three at the same time.' Evaluate this statement, considering more than one point of view.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument acknowledging the genuine philosophical difficulty (one substance, three persons is logically complex; modalism and polytheism are both errors), then arguing why Christians still affirm it (scriptural evidence; lived experience of Father, Son and Spirit; historic creeds). Includes a non-religious or sceptical view (Dawkins-style critique: the Trinity is incoherent) alongside a theological defence. Clear, reasoned conclusion. Secure: Both sides addressed; some use of evidence; conclusion reached but not fully justified. Developing: One-sided argument with a brief nod to the other view; limited use of sources. Emerging: Simple personal opinion with no engagement with evidence or opposing views.

practice_questions.text: Give two names Sikhs use for God.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two of: Waheguru; Satnam; Akal Purakh; Kartapurkh; Ik Onkar (acceptable as a statement about God's oneness).

practice_questions.text: What does the Sikh term 'mukti' mean?
practice_questions.marks: Two marks for: liberation from the cycle of rebirth — the soul's union with God. One mark for: 'freedom' or 'salvation' without further explanation.

practice_questions.text: Describe Sikh beliefs about the nature of God.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Detailed description covering: God as one (Ik Onkar); God as immanent and all-pervading (GGS 1); God as personal, creator and Guru (GGS 294); key qualities from Mool Mantar (truth, fearless, without hate, timeless, beyond birth and death); self-revealing through grace. Secure: Clear description with at least three qualities and textual reference. Developing: Basic description of God as one with limited detail. Emerging: Simple statement that Sikhs believe in one God.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the belief in 'simran' influences the daily life of a Sikh.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains simran as meditating on God's name (Nam); link to GGS 125 and the gurmukh; influences: early morning prayers (Nitnem — five daily prayers); use of 'Waheguru' as a devotional focus; Sikh congregational worship (sangat) including kirtan (devotional singing); connection of meditation to sewa and honest living. Secure: Clear explanation of simran with two developed examples of influence. Developing: Basic explanation of simran; limited influence. Emerging: Brief mention of prayer or worship.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Sikh beliefs about the purpose of human life.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Belief 1: Human life is a precious opportunity to achieve mukti (liberation) through turning to God — GGS 2 teaches that without God's name, human birth is wasted. Belief 2: The purpose is to become a gurmukh rather than a manmukh — GGS 125 teaches that the gurmukh who meditates on God's name attains liberation. Could also develop the three duties (Nam Japna, Kirat Karni, Vand Chakna). Secure: Two beliefs explained with at least one textual reference. Developing: Two beliefs stated; underdeveloped or lacking a source. Emerging: One belief with little development.

practice_questions.text:
'Sikhs do not need to go to a place of worship to find God, because God is present everywhere.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Agrees: Sikhism teaches God is immanent and all-pervading (GGS 1); simran can be practised anywhere; the three duties — Nam Japna, Kirat Karni, Vand Chakna — are lived in daily life, not only in the gurdwara; Guru Nanak rejected external ritual as a substitute for inner devotion. Disagrees: The gurdwara is the central place of Sikh community (sangat); communal worship, kirtan and langar are commanded forms of Sikh practice; the Guru Granth Sahib is kept in the gurdwara; corporate worship strengthens the community. Non-religious view: A Humanist might agree that community can be found anywhere without the need for a sacred building, but the social function of religious community still has value. Justified conclusion. Secure: Two developed arguments with at least one source; some evaluation. Developing: Some points on both sides; limited evaluation. Emerging: Descriptive or one-sided.

practice_questions.text: Give two aims of punishment.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of any two from: justice, retribution, deterrence, reformation. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: What is meant by 'absolute morality'?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear, precise definition stating that absolute morality holds that right and wrong are fixed and never change regardless of circumstances or culture.
Secure: A reasonable definition noting that some actions are always right or wrong.
Developing: A vague or partially correct definition.
Emerging: Little relevant content.

practice_questions.text: Describe the work of prison chaplains and one religious group that supports offenders.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Detailed description of prison chaplains offering pastoral care, counselling and religious support to prisoners; accurate description of the Angulimala Society (Buddhist charity) working in British prisons through meditation and compassionate support, with a clear link to Buddhist belief in rehabilitation.
Secure: Accurate description of both prison chaplains and one religious group with some development.
Developing: Basic description of one of the above with limited development.
Emerging: Simple reference with little detail. [5 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two beliefs from different religious traditions about the purpose of punishment.
In your answer, refer to a source of wisdom or authority for each tradition.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two fully developed beliefs from two different traditions, each linked to a named and interpreted source of authority (e.g. Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 for Judaism; CCC 2266–2267 for Catholicism). Clear explanation of how the source supports the belief.
Secure: Two beliefs from different traditions, each with a relevant source, though one or both may lack full interpretation.
Developing: One developed belief with a source, or two beliefs without adequate source reference.
Emerging: Simple points without development or sources. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two contrasting religious views on capital punishment.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly contrasting views (e.g. a tradition that may permit capital punishment under strict conditions vs. one that opposes it entirely), both developed and supported with named sources. Genuine contrast explained.
Secure: Two contrasting views with sources, though development may be uneven.
Developing: Two views identified but contrast not fully developed.
Emerging: One view or very limited development. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Reformation is the most important aim of punishment.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to religious teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Many Christian traditions emphasise that punishment should restore the offender — prison chaplains embody this.
• Buddhism values reformation through compassion (karuna) and the example of Milarepa and Angulimala.
• Humanists argue that reducing reoffending (reformation) is the most empirically effective aim.

Arguments against:
• Islam and Judaism also value justice and retribution as divine commands that must be satisfied.
• Victims and communities may feel that justice without retribution is incomplete.
• Deterrence is valued across many traditions as preventing future harm to society.

Mastering: Sophisticated, balanced argument; at least two traditions engaged; non-religious view included; clear and justified personal conclusion.
Secure: Two developed points of view with religious references and a conclusion.
Developing: Some argument with limited balance or weak conclusion.
Emerging: One-sided or very limited response. [15 marks + SPaG 5%]

practice_questions.text: Give two purposes of marriage in a religious tradition.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each valid purpose from any tradition, e.g.: companionship / mutual support; procreation and raising of children (Christian); fulfilling one's duty in the householder ashrama (Hindu); a sign of God's mercy — Qur'an 30:21 (Islam); a sacramental covenant before God (Catholic). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: What is the ketubah in Jewish marriage?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise definition that the ketubah is a Jewish marriage contract that sets out the husband's obligations to his wife, traditionally read aloud at the wedding ceremony.
Secure: A broadly accurate definition.
Developing: Partial — knows it is a document but limited detail.
Emerging: Incorrect or no relevant content.

practice_questions.text: Describe the Sikh Anand Karaj ceremony and explain its religious significance.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate description of the couple walking around the Guru Granth Sahib four times as the four lavans (GGS 773–774) are sung; clear explanation that each circuit deepens the couple's spiritual commitment and that marriage is understood as a shared spiritual journey in the presence of scripture.
Secure: Accurate description with some explanation of significance.
Developing: Basic description of the ceremony without explanation of significance.
Emerging: Very limited content. [5 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two religious beliefs about the purpose of marriage.
In your answer, refer to a source of wisdom or authority for each belief.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two developed beliefs from two traditions, each with a named and interpreted source (e.g. Mark 10:6–8 for Christianity; Qur'an 30:21 for Islam; GGS 773–774 / the Anand Karaj for Sikhism; Sigalovada Sutta for Buddhism). Full development of what the source teaches and why it matters.
Secure: Two beliefs with sources, one or both developed.
Developing: One developed belief with source, or two without adequate sources.
Emerging: Simple points only. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two contrasting religious views on cohabitation (living together outside marriage).
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two genuinely contrasting views (e.g. Catholic opposition grounded in CCC and the view that sexual intimacy belongs within the sacrament of marriage, vs. a Buddhist or non-religious acceptance that committed cohabitation can be as ethically valid as formal marriage). Both developed with sources; contrast clearly drawn.
Secure: Two contrasting views developed, contrast noted.
Developing: Two views without genuine contrast.
Emerging: One view or very limited development. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Marriage should be for life, whatever the circumstances.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to religious teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Catholic Christianity: marriage is a sacrament and is indissoluble (CCC 2360–2363); divorce is not recognised.
• Sikhism: the Anand Karaj makes marriage a lifelong spiritual union in the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib.
• Islam: Qur'an 30:21 presents marriage as God's design for peace and mercy; family stability is a high value.

Arguments against:
• Many Protestant and some Jewish traditions permit divorce in cases of adultery, abuse or irretrievable breakdown.
• Buddhism does not prohibit divorce; reducing suffering (avoiding dukkha) may justify ending an unhappy marriage.
• Humanists argue that a relationship's value lies in its quality, not its legal permanence; forcing people to remain in harmful marriages causes harm.

Mastering: Sophisticated, balanced evaluation; multiple traditions engaged; non-religious view included; clear justified personal conclusion.
Secure: Two developed viewpoints with references; conclusion present.
Developing: Some argument; limited balance or weak conclusion.
Emerging: One-sided or minimal. [15 marks. Spelling, punctuation and grammar carry extra marks on specified extended-writing questions.]

practice_questions.text: Give two attributes of God in Catholic belief.
practice_questions.marks: One mark per accurate attribute, up to two. Examples: omnipotence (all-powerful), omnibenevolence (all-good), omniscience (all-knowing), omnipresence (present everywhere). Mastering: two precise attributes with correct terminology. Emerging: one vague point.

practice_questions.text: What does 'imago Dei' mean in Catholic teaching?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: imago Dei (Latin for 'image of God') is the teaching from Genesis 1:26-28 that every human being reflects something of the divine nature and therefore possesses inherent dignity. Secure: accurate one-sentence definition. Emerging: 'made in God's image' without further explanation.

practice_questions.text: Describe Catholic teaching about the Trinity.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5): detailed description including the three persons (Father, Son, Holy Spirit), key scripture for each (Luke 15:11-32, John 1:1-3/14, Galatians 5:22-23), Augustine's De Trinitate, the Nicene Creed formulation, and the significance — one God, not three. Secure (3-4): clear account of three persons with some scripture. Developing (2): names three persons without development. Emerging (1): simple statement that Catholics believe in three persons.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Catholic beliefs about human nature.
Refer to a source of Catholic teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7-8): two well-developed beliefs, each linked to scripture or named theologian. Examples: (1) Humans are made in the image of God (imago Dei, Genesis 1:26-28); this means every person has inherent dignity, rationality and the capacity for relationship with God; it grounds Catholic opposition to anything that treats a person as less than fully human. (2) Original sin (Genesis 2-3) means human nature is damaged by the first disobedience; all people inherit a tendency towards sin; this is why baptism is necessary — it cleanses original sin and restores the person to grace. Aquinas also stressed that despite original sin, human nature is essentially good and oriented towards God. Secure (5-6): two beliefs with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two undeveloped. Emerging (1-2): simple statements.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which the doctrine of creation ex nihilo influences Catholic belief and practice.
Refer to a source of Catholic teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7-8): two well-developed influences. Examples: (1) Creation ex nihilo (Augustine, Confessions XII, 7) establishes God's complete sovereignty — nothing exists independently of God's will; this grounds Catholic worship and prayer as a response of total dependence on God. (2) Because God created everything from nothing, all creation is good and reflects God's glory; this underpins Catholic care for the environment and the tradition of seeking God through the beauty of creation. Secure (5-6): two influences with some development. Developing (3-4): one developed point. Emerging (1-2): simple statements.

practice_questions.text:
'The doctrine of original sin is the most important Catholic teaching about humanity.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Catholic teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: original sin explains the human condition — why people struggle to do good even when they know what is right (Romans 7 resonance); it is the basis for the necessity of baptism and salvation through Christ; without it, the Incarnation and the crucifixion have no doctrinal rationale; it shapes Catholic sacramental life. Arguments against: imago Dei could be seen as equally foundational — it establishes every person's dignity and is the basis for Catholic social teaching, human rights and opposition to injustice; Aquinas's teaching that human nature is essentially good is arguably more central to how Catholics engage with ethics; the Trinity and the Incarnation could be considered more central doctrines because they define who God is and how salvation works. Conclusion: justified personal view weighing the relative importance. Mastering (13-15): sustained argument, precise sources, clear conclusion. Secure (9-12): two sides with some source use. Developing (5-8): one-sided. Emerging (1-4): descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Give two purposes of punishment recognised by the Catholic Church.
practice_questions.marks: Award one mark for each correct purpose, up to two. Acceptable answers include: retribution (just desert for wrongdoing) / deterrence (preventing future crime) / rehabilitation / reformation (reforming the offender) / protection of society / restoration of public order (Catechism 2266).

practice_questions.text: What is the current Catholic teaching on capital punishment?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The death penalty is 'inadmissible' in all circumstances because it is an attack on the inviolable dignity of the human person (Catechism 2267, revised by Pope Francis in 2018). The Church works for its global abolition.
Secure: Capital punishment is inadmissible according to the updated Catechism (2018).
Developing: The Catholic Church is against capital punishment.
Emerging: Catholics don't like the death penalty.

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between crime and sin in Catholic moral teaching.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A detailed description covering: crime breaks the law of the state and carries legal punishment; sin breaks the moral law of God and damages the relationship with God, others and oneself (CCC 1849); the two overlap but are not identical — some sins (envy) are not crimes; some legal acts may be sinful; Catholic moral reasoning uses Natural Law, an absolutist approach developed by Aquinas, to judge acts independently of state law.
Secure: A clear description of the distinction with at least one example and some theological grounding.
Developing: A basic description identifying that crime is legal and sin is religious, without examples or theological depth.
Emerging: Vague reference to laws and religion.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the Catholic Church's teaching on forgiveness influences attitudes towards crime and punishment.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A developed explanation covering: Jesus taught unlimited forgiveness (Matthew 18:21–22 — 'seventy-seven times'), meaning victims are called to release resentment and not seek vengeance; Matthew 6:14–15 links human forgiveness to receiving God's forgiveness; forgiveness at the personal level does not eliminate the need for justice at the social level — the Church supports just punishment while insisting on the offender's dignity; Catholic prison chaplains embody this by combining support for victims with concern for offenders' rehabilitation.
Secure: Two or more clear influences explained with scriptural reference.
Developing: One influence without depth.
Emerging: Brief mention of forgiveness.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which Catholic teaching on capital punishment has developed.
Refer to a source of Catholic teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two well-developed points with named sources. Point 1: the earlier tradition (e.g. Augustine, Letters 134 and 153 to Macedonius) accepted capital punishment as a legitimate state function and even an act of mercy; Evangelium Vitae 56 (Pope John Paul II, 1995) significantly narrowed this, arguing that cases in which it was truly necessary were 'very rare, if not practically non-existent' in modern societies with secure incarceration. Point 2: Pope Francis revised Catechism 2267 in 2018 to declare the death penalty 'inadmissible' in all circumstances, as an attack on the inviolable dignity of the person — a decisive development that commits the Church to working for global abolition.
Secure: Two points explained with sources.
Developing: One point well explained, second superficial.
Emerging: One brief point.

practice_questions.text:
'The Catholic Church's opposition to capital punishment is inconsistent with earlier Catholic tradition.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Catholic teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• For much of its history the Church accepted capital punishment as a legitimate state function — Augustine (Letters 134 and 153 to Macedonius) and later Aquinas both allowed for its use.
• The Old Testament contains explicit support for the death penalty as divine law (Genesis 9:6: 'Whoever sheds human blood, by humans shall their blood be shed'; Exodus 21:24).
• Critics of the development, including some conservative Catholic theologians, argue that the 2018 revision of CCC 2267 contradicts settled doctrine and is therefore inconsistent.

Arguments against:
• The Church teaches that doctrinal development (as articulated by John Henry Newman) is legitimate: the core principle (human dignity) has not changed, but its implications for the death penalty have been worked out more fully over time.
• Evangelium Vitae 56 (1995) did not absolutely condemn capital punishment but already significantly narrowed its acceptable use, showing that the direction of travel was consistent before 2018.
• The revised CCC 2267 grounds its opposition in the doctrine of 'imago Dei' (Genesis 1:26–27) — the inviolable dignity of every human person — which is a continuous Catholic principle, not a new one.
• Modern conditions (secure incarceration, human rights law, the risk of executing the innocent) make the practical case against capital punishment very strong on grounds the Church has always accepted.

Conclusion: A justified conclusion should assess whether the 2018 development represents a genuine inconsistency (change of substance) or a legitimate development (change of emphasis while core principles remain). Most Catholic theologians argue the latter.

Mastering: Sophisticated argument with named sources and clear justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides developed with some sources and a conclusion.
Developing: One-sided or conclusion missing.
Emerging: Simple statements without reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Give two reasons why the Catholic Church opposes abortion.
practice_questions.marks: Award one mark for each of two correct reasons from: the embryo has full human dignity from fertilisation / life is sacred (imago Dei) / Catechism 2270 teaches life must be protected from conception / God has sovereignty over life and death.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by 'creation ex nihilo'?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: God created the universe from absolutely nothing, without pre-existing material. Secure: God made everything from nothing. Developing: Vague — 'God created the world' without the key phrase 'from nothing'. Emerging: Incomplete or confused answer.

practice_questions.text: Describe Catholic beliefs about the value of human life from conception to natural death.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Describes imago Dei as the basis of human dignity; references Catechism 2270 on abortion and Evangelium Vitae 65 on euthanasia; explains what the sanctity of life means in practice (opposition to abortion, euthanasia, support for palliative care). Secure: Two or more of the above with some explanation and reference to at least one source. Developing: General Catholic opposition stated without explanation of why or use of sources. Emerging: Simple statement — 'life is precious' — with no religious grounding.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Pope John Paul II's 1996 Message to the Pontifical Academy of Sciences addressed the relationship between Catholic faith and evolution.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains that paragraphs 3 and 4 affirmed evolution as 'more than a hypothesis'; explains the distinction between the body (subject to evolution) and the soul (directly created by God); explains why this was significant (showing faith and science are not simply opposed). Secure: Correct reference to the 1996 message; clear distinction between Catholic acceptance of biological evolution and insistence on the soul's divine origin. Developing: Vague reference to the Church accepting evolution without the soul distinction. Emerging: No clear reference to the document or its content.

practice_questions.text: Explain two Catholic beliefs about creation that are drawn from the Genesis accounts.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two distinct beliefs (e.g. creation ex nihilo from Genesis 1:1-3; imago Dei from Genesis 1:26-27), each explained with the relevant passage and its theological significance. Clear, well-developed paragraphs. Secure: Two beliefs identified and linked to Genesis with explanation. Developing: One belief explained; second underdeveloped. Emerging: General reference to Genesis without specific beliefs or passages.

practice_questions.text: 'Science has made belief in a creator God unnecessary.' Evaluate this statement from a Catholic perspective, considering more than one point of view.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Argues the scientific view (Hawking's Big Bang; Dawkins' blind evolution) with precision; responds with the Catholic position (science and faith answer different questions; theistic evolution; the soul's origin; Augustine on ex nihilo). Includes a Humanist/secular perspective and a theological counter. Clear personal conclusion. Secure: Both sides addressed; some use of named sources (Hawking, Dawkins, Church documents); conclusion reached. Developing: One-sided with a brief nod to the other view. Emerging: Simple personal opinion with no engagement with evidence.

practice_questions.text: Give two qualities of Allah described in the Qur'an.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two named qualities: All-Knowing (Al-'Alim), Most Merciful (Al-Rahman), Most Compassionate (Al-Rahim), All-Seeing (Al-Basir), All-Hearing (Al-Sami'), immanent, transcendent, omnipotent. Accept qualities with or without Arabic names.

practice_questions.text: What is tawhid?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: The Islamic doctrine of the absolute oneness and uniqueness of Allah — the foundational belief of Islam, confirmed in Qur'an 3:18, meaning nothing in creation can be compared or associated with Allah. Developing: The belief that Allah is one God.

practice_questions.text: Describe how Muslims show respect for the Qur'an and explain why they do so.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two or more practices (wudu before touching, storing on a high shelf, not placing on floor, using a Qur'an stand, careful handling) with explanation rooted in belief that it is the direct uncreated word of Allah. Secure: Two practices with one clear reason. Developing: One practice with limited explanation. Emerging: Vague reference to the Qur'an being holy.

practice_questions.text: Explain how belief in tawhid influences Muslim worship and daily life.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Links tawhid (Qur'an 3:18) to prohibition of images (guards against shirk), direction of all prayer to Allah alone, the Shahadah as declaration of tawhid, Islamic calligraphy replacing figurative art. Secure: Two clear influences with explanation. Developing: One influence with limited connection to tawhid. Emerging: Vague mention of Muslims believing in one God.

practice_questions.text: Explain two Islamic beliefs about the Qur'an and its importance for Muslims.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two beliefs each developed with a named source. e.g. (1) The Qur'an is the direct word of Allah revealed through Jibril (Qur'an 2:97-98) — therefore it is perfect and unalterable, superseding all previous scriptures; (2) The Qur'an is a guide for all of life, not just worship — it covers law, ethics, family, and justice. Secure: Two beliefs with at least one source cited and interpreted. Developing: Two beliefs stated; sources absent. Emerging: One belief only.

practice_questions.text: 'The Qur'an is the most important source of guidance for Muslims.' Evaluate this statement, referring to Islamic teachings and non-religious perspectives.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Structured argument. Agree: Qur'an is the direct word of Allah, primary source of sharia, memorised in its entirety by millions (hafiz); Qur'an 2:97-98 confirms divine origin. Disagree: Hadith and Sunnah are essential to interpret the Qur'an — many practices (how to pray, how to fast) are detailed in the Hadith, not the Qur'an itself; some Muslims emphasise the role of scholarly consensus (ijma) and analogy (qiyas) alongside the texts. Non-religious view: no text is divinely revealed; the Qur'an is a human document of historical and literary value. Clear justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides with at least two sources; conclusion present. Developing: One-sided or weak sources. Emerging: Simple assertion.

practice_questions.text: Give two ways in which religious believers promote human dignity in practice.

[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how the concept of imago Dei shapes Christian teaching on human rights.
practice_questions.marks:

practice_questions.text:
Explain two religious teachings that emphasise the value and dignity of every human life.
Refer to sources of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct teachings from different traditions, each with a named source and interpretation. E.g. Genesis 1:26-27 (imago Dei — made in God's image so every life is sacred); Qur'an 5:32 (saving one life is like saving all of humanity — grounds Islamic human rights ethics); Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 (saving one life saves an entire world — underpins Jewish tzedakah). Each developed with explanation.
Secure: Two teachings with named sources; adequate explanation.
Developing: Two teachings; one developed.
Emerging: One teaching, limited development. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two contrasting views on whether religious believers should follow the law of the land when it conflicts with their faith.
Refer to sources of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: View 1 — religious conviction may require civil disobedience when law is unjust (Martin Luther King's Letter from Birmingham Jail; the tradition of conscientious objection; prophetic tradition of challenging unjust laws). View 2 — most religious traditions teach respect for civil authority (Romans 13:1 for Christians; Islamic principle of following legitimate authority; Sikh legal cases resolved through courts rather than disobedience). Both views developed with named sources.
Secure: Two contrasting views each with a source; clear explanation.
Developing: Two views; limited source use.
Emerging: One view described. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Religious freedom should never be restricted by the laws of a country.'
Evaluate this statement, considering more than one point of view. Refer to religion and belief in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support: Article 18 UDHR protects religious freedom as a fundamental right; all traditions affirm the right to practise faith; Sikhs won legal cases to wear religious items; persecution of religious minorities shows the harm caused when states suppress faith; Humanists also support Article 18 as a universal right.
Arguments against: Religious freedom can conflict with others' rights (e.g. a registrar refusing same-sex ceremonies); religious extremism shows that unlimited religious freedom can enable harm; courts have legitimately limited religious expression that incites hatred; the common good (Catholic concept, Catechism 1905-1912) sometimes requires individual freedoms to be balanced against community welfare.
Conclusion: Most traditions accept some limits on freedom when it harms others, but the default should be maximum freedom. Humanists and most religious traditions agree that no one should face persecution for their beliefs.
Mastering: Sustained argument, both sides, named sources including Article 18 UDHR, justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides with sources; conclusion reached.
Developing: One side stronger; limited sources.
Emerging: One-sided; few sources. [15 marks + 6 SPaG]

practice_questions.text: Give two attributes of G-d that Jewish people believe in.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each correct attribute: any two from omnipotent, omnipresent, omnibenevolent, eternal, transcendent, merciful, judge.

practice_questions.text: What is the Shema?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: The central declaration of Jewish faith drawn from Deuteronomy 6:4 — 'Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one' — recited morning and evening by observant Jews. Developing: A Jewish prayer declaring belief in one God.

practice_questions.text: Describe the main features of a synagogue and explain their religious significance.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Identifies three or more features (aron hakodesh, ner tamid, bimah, Ten Commandments display) with explanation of significance for each (e.g. ner tamid represents G-d's constant presence). Secure: Two features with some explanation of significance. Developing: One or two features, description only, little explanation. Emerging: Vague reference to the synagogue as a place of prayer.

practice_questions.text: Explain how belief in G-d's transcendence influences Jewish practices.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Links transcendence (Isaiah 55:8-9) to specific practices: prohibition of images, writing G-d as 'G-d', not pronouncing YHWH, the concept of G-d being beyond human understanding. Secure: Two practices linked to transcendence with explanation. Developing: One practice with limited connection to the belief. Emerging: Vague mention of transcendence without linking to practice.

practice_questions.text: Explain two Jewish beliefs about G-d's nature, using sources of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed beliefs each with a named source. e.g. (1) G-d is transcendent — Isaiah 55:8-9 says G-d's ways are higher than human ways, which is why images are forbidden; (2) G-d is the eternal judge — reward and punishment are built into the moral order, seen in the High Holy Days. Secure: Two beliefs explained with at least one source cited and interpreted. Developing: Two beliefs named but not developed; sources absent. Emerging: One belief only, no sources.

practice_questions.text: 'The synagogue is more important than the home for Jewish worship.' Evaluate this statement, referring to Jewish teachings and non-religious perspectives.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Structured argument. Agree: synagogue is the communal centre for prayer, Torah reading, and lifecycle events; Orthodox Judaism requires minyan (quorum of ten) for certain prayers. Disagree: home is where Shabbat is observed, mezuzah marks sacred space, and faith is transmitted to children; historically, synagogues were not always available (diaspora). Non-religious view: neither has spiritual significance; community and family bonds are equally achievable without religious buildings or rituals. Clear justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides with two or more sources; conclusion present. Developing: One-sided or weak sources. Emerging: Simple assertion.

practice_questions.text: Give two Catholic beliefs about what happens to a person after death.
practice_questions.marks: Award one mark for each correct belief, up to two marks. Acceptable answers include: the soul is judged at the moment of death (particular judgement) / the person may go to heaven, hell or purgatory / at the Last Judgement the body will be resurrected / the whole person (body and soul) will share in eternal life / those in purgatory are purified before entering heaven.

practice_questions.text: What does the Catholic Church mean by 'purgatory'?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: The state of purification after death for those who die in God's grace but are not yet fully purified; the process that enables them to achieve the holiness necessary to enter heaven. The Catechism (CCC 1030) affirms it and connects it to 1 Corinthians 3:11–15.
Secure: A state after death where souls are cleansed before entering heaven.
Developing: A place between heaven and hell.
Emerging: Something to do with the afterlife.

practice_questions.text: Describe Catholic teaching on the resurrection of the body.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A detailed description covering: the resurrection of the body is a core Catholic dogma, based on 1 Corinthians 15 (Paul's argument that Christ's resurrection guarantees the resurrection of believers); the resurrection body is 'spiritual' and glorified, not a simple resuscitation; the whole person (body and soul) shares in eternal life; the Catechism (CCC 988–989) affirms bodily resurrection as inseparable from faith in Christ's own resurrection.
Secure: A clear account with reference to 1 Corinthians 15 and the distinction between physical resurrection and the survival of the soul alone.
Developing: Basic description without scriptural reference.
Emerging: Vague reference to life after death.

practice_questions.text: Explain how Catholic teaching on the sanctity of life influences attitudes towards palliative care.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A developed explanation covering: the Church teaches that human life has inherent dignity as a gift from God (Genesis 1:26–27); this means life must be respected from conception to natural death; palliative care is supported because it relieves suffering without deliberately ending life; Catholic hospices (e.g. St Joseph's Hospice, Hackney) embody this principle; the distinction between ordinary and extraordinary means of treatment allows refusal of futile interventions; suffering can be redemptive when united with Christ (Evangelium Vitae 65, Salvifici Doloris).
Secure: Two or more clear influences explained with theological grounding.
Developing: One influence described but not well developed.
Emerging: Brief mention without explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Catholic beliefs about heaven and hell.
Refer to a source of Catholic teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two fully developed beliefs with named sources. Belief 1 on heaven: described in CCC 1024 as 'perfect life with the Most Holy Trinity'; Jesus promised 'In my Father's house are many rooms' (John 14:2); it is a gift of grace, not earned merit, offered to those who die in God's friendship. Belief 2 on hell: described in CCC 1033 as the state of permanent separation from God, resulting from the free and final rejection of God's love; the parable of Lazarus and the rich man (Luke 16:19–31) depicts both states as fixed after death.
Secure: Two beliefs clearly explained, each with a source of authority.
Developing: One belief well explained; the second is superficial or lacks a source.
Emerging: One brief point without development or source.

practice_questions.text:
'Catholics should support the legalisation of assisted dying because it reduces suffering.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Catholic teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Non-religious thinkers argue that if a person is suffering intolerably and there is no prospect of recovery, continuing to live is cruel rather than dignified.
• 'Dignity in Dying' and some secular ethicists argue that autonomy — the right to choose the manner of one's death — is a fundamental human right.
• Peter Singer's 'quality of life' argument holds that when life no longer has value to the person living it, ending it is compassionate, not wrong.

Arguments against:
• The Catholic Church teaches that euthanasia is a 'grave violation of the law of God' (Evangelium Vitae 65, John Paul II, 1995) because it involves deliberately ending a life that belongs ultimately to God.
• Every human being bears the 'imago Dei' (Genesis 1:26–27) — an inherent dignity that suffering does not diminish; this is not a quality that can be lost.
• Palliative care can manage most terminal pain without deliberately ending life; the Church argues this is always the appropriate alternative.
• The 'double effect' principle allows pain relief that may shorten life as a side-effect, so the Church's position does not require patients to suffer unnecessarily.

Conclusion: A justified conclusion should weigh the Humanist appeal to autonomy and compassion against the Catholic insistence on the sanctity of life and the availability of palliative alternatives.

Mastering: Sophisticated argument with named sources and clear, justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides with some sources and a conclusion.
Developing: One-sided or conclusion missing.
Emerging: Simple statements without reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Give two examples of moral evil.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two plausible examples of evil caused by human choice: murder; war; racism; cruelty; theft; oppression; torture. Two marks maximum.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'Original Sin' in Catholic teaching?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: The state of sin and separation from God into which all human beings are born, resulting from the first disobedience of Adam and Eve; it describes a damaged condition of human nature — a tendency towards self-centredness and a weakening of the will — not personal guilt for Adam's act. Secure: A fallen state all humans are born into due to Adam and Eve's disobedience. Developing: When Adam and Eve sinned and passed it on. Emerging: A kind of sin people are born with.

practice_questions.text: Describe Augustine's teaching that evil is a privation of the good.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Detailed description of Augustine's argument in Enchiridion 3:11 — God created all things good; evil is not a substance but an absence or corruption of the good that should be present (e.g. blindness is the absence of sight; cruelty is the corruption of love); this preserves God's goodness because God did not create evil; evil enters through creaturely freedom misused. Reference to Original Sin as privation of original integrity. Secure: Two features with one explained significance. Developing: Basic description of privation with one example. Emerging: Simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain the influence of the doctrine of Original Sin on Catholic practice.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains that Original Sin means all humans are born in a damaged state (weakened will, darkened intellect); this influences the practice of baptism (the sacrament that removes Original Sin and restores the person to grace); influences the practice of confession (Sacrament of Reconciliation — responding to actual sins that follow from the fallen condition); shapes Catholic moral education (recognising human weakness while insisting on the possibility of grace). Reference to the Catechism or Genesis 3. Secure: Two developed points of influence. Developing: One developed point. Emerging: Simple statement.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Catholic responses to the problem of evil and suffering.
Refer to a source of Catholic teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed responses, each with source and interpretation. Response 1: Free will defence — God gave humans genuine freedom; freedom requires the possibility of choosing wrong; moral evil results from human choice, not God's will; God is good but respects human freedom. Response 2: Suffering can have redemptive meaning when united with Christ's suffering — Salvifici Doloris 13 and 23 (John Paul II, 1984); Isaiah 53 (Suffering Servant fulfilled in Christ); suffering is not meaningless but can be spiritually fruitful. Each response with source and significance. Secure: Two responses with one source. Developing: One developed response. Emerging: Simple statement.

practice_questions.text:
'The existence of evil proves that God does not exist.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to Catholic teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: The logical problem of evil (Mackie): if God is omnipotent, omniscient and omnibenevolent, there should be no evil; since evil exists, such a God cannot. Natural evil especially seems hard to reconcile with a loving Creator — earthquake victims include the innocent. The scale and gratuitousness of suffering (e.g. the Holocaust, cancer in children) seems incompatible with divine love. Arguments against: The free will defence maintains that God allows evil as the cost of creating genuinely free moral beings who can love. Augustine's privation theory argues evil is not created by God but is an absence of good — so evil's existence does not imply God created it. Salvifici Doloris and Isaiah 53 show evil and suffering can be transformed through Christ's Cross — they become occasions of grace, not disproof of God. The soul-making view (Irenaeus) argues suffering is the condition for moral growth. Non-religious view: Atheists argue the problem of evil is strong evidence against God, though some (e.g. secular philosophers) acknowledge the logical problem is not conclusive — the question is one of probability and moral intuition. Conclusion: A strong answer will argue the problem of evil is a serious challenge that Catholic theology has engaged with, not ignored — the free will defence and redemptive suffering together form a partial but not fully satisfying response. Whether the challenge is decisive depends on prior commitments about the nature of God. Mastering: Sustained two-sided argument, named sources interpreted, justified conclusion. Secure: Two sides, one source. Developing: One side. Emerging: Simple view.

practice_questions.text: Give two religious concepts that support environmental responsibility.

Secure: At least two specific teachings with some development.

Emerging: Simple statement only.

Secure: Two points with some development.

Emerging: Simple statement about Islam and environment.

Explain two contrasting religious and non-religious views about the origin of the universe.
Refer to sources of authority in your answer.

Mastering: One religious view (e.g. Christian Genesis 1 with Genesis 1:28 or Qur'an 36:81 or Sikh Mool Mantar) and one non-religious view (Big Bang theory — Hawking; blind evolution — Dawkins) each developed with source, explanation of significance and acknowledgement of where they may conflict or complement each other.
Secure: Two contrasting views, at least one source, some development.

practice_questions.text:
'Science has made religious accounts of creation unnecessary.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to religious teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• The Big Bang theory (Hawking) provides a scientific account of cosmic origins without requiring a creator.
• Darwin's evolution by natural selection explains the diversity of life without design or purpose.
• Dawkins argues that 'blind evolution' shows the appearance of design in nature can be explained entirely naturalistically.
• Humanist Climate Action draws on environmental ethics without requiring a religious framework.
Arguments against:
• Many believers argue science and religion answer different questions — science asks 'how?', religion asks 'why?' — so they cannot make each other unnecessary.
• Pope John Paul II (1996) affirmed that evolution and Catholic faith are compatible, showing religious thinkers engage seriously with science rather than ignoring it.
• Religious stewardship frameworks (khalifah, tikkun olam, Laudato Si') provide moral motivations for environmental action that science alone does not provide.
• Buddhist paticca-samuppada is consistent with scientific accounts of dependent causation — Buddhism never claimed a creator God to be displaced.
Conclusion: Justified personal judgement.
Mastering: Two sides, multiple sources, non-religious view, clear justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides, one source, conclusion.
Developing: One side stronger.
Emerging: One-sided, no conclusion.

Includes a non-Buddhist or secular view. Clear, reasoned personal conclusion. Secure: Both sides addressed with some use of Buddhist concepts; conclusion reached. Developing: One-sided with brief nod to other view. Emerging: Simple personal opinion.

practice_questions.text: What does 'langar' mean in Sikhism?

One mark for: 'free food at the gurdwara' or 'community kitchen' without explanation of significance.

practice_questions.text: Describe the features and importance of the langar in the gurdwara.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Features: free vegetarian meal; prepared and served by volunteers as sewa; open to all regardless of background; everyone sits together on the floor in rows; introduced by Guru Nanak. Importance: expresses Sikh equality (all eat together); challenges caste dining restrictions; embodies sewa; Guru Granth Sahib (p.349) teaches that caste counts for nothing before God, which langar puts into practice. Secure: Clear description with features and some importance. Developing: Describes langar as a free meal without much detail on importance. Emerging: Brief mention of a free meal.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the Amrit Sanskar ceremony influences the life of a Khalsa Sikh.

Shows how the ceremony shapes daily practice and Sikh identity. Secure: Clear explanation of ceremony and at least two developed influences. Developing: Basic description of ceremony; limited influence. Emerging: Mentions the Five Ks without connecting to the ceremony.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which the Guru Granth Sahib is central to Sikh worship.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Way 1: The Guru Granth Sahib is the living Guru — Guru Gobind Singh declared it the eternal Guru in 1708; it is installed on a throne, carried in procession, and read aloud; the Hukamnama provides daily guidance. Way 2: The Guru Granth Sahib structures community worship — kirtan (hymn-singing), Ardas, karah prashad all centre on the scripture; the Hukamnama read from the Guru Granth Sahib gives the congregation guidance for the day. Secure: Two ways explained with at least one textual reference. Developing: Two ways stated; underdeveloped or lacking a source. Emerging: One way with little development.

practice_questions.text:
'Wearing the Five Ks is the most important way a Sikh shows their faith.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Agrees: the Five Ks are a visible external commitment to the Khalsa; they mark a Sikh as distinctive; wearing Kesh and Kirpan can involve real social challenges in a non-Sikh society; they were given by Guru Gobind Singh as part of the Amrit Sanskar. Disagrees: not all Sikhs take Amrit or wear the Five Ks (Sahajdhari Sikhs); the Guru Granth Sahib teaches that inner devotion (simran, sewa) matters more than external forms; Guru Nanak criticised empty ritual; daily practices of Nam Japna, Kirat Karni and Vand Chakna may be more day-to-day expressions of faith. Non-religious view: a Humanist would argue that commitment to equality and service (langar, sewa) expresses values more meaningfully than dress. Justified conclusion. Secure: Two developed arguments with at least one source; some evaluation. Developing: Some points on both sides; limited evaluation. Emerging: Descriptive or one-sided.

practice_questions.text: Give two religious reasons why a believer might oppose euthanasia.
practice_questions.marks: Award one mark for each of two correctly grounded reasons from: God gives and takes life (any religion) / human life is made in God's image (Christianity) / pikuach nefesh — preserving life is a supreme duty (Judaism) / life is a trust from Allah, only He can take it (Islam) / first Precept — do not take life (Buddhism) / ahimsa — non-violence (Hinduism / Sikhism). Must be a religious reason, not a general objection.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the 'sanctity of life'?

practice_questions.text: Describe Jewish beliefs about the value of human life, including beliefs about abortion.
