practice_questions.text: Explain two contrasting views on abortion — one religious and one non-religious.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Religious view fully developed with source (e.g. Catholic: Catechism 2270, imago Dei, life from conception; or Islamic: Qur'an 6:151, ensoulment via Qur'an 32:9, only Allah has sovereignty over life). Non-religious view fully developed (e.g. Peter Singer's speciesism — capacity for conscious experience matters more than species; or Humanist autonomy — the woman's right to choose). Each view clearly explained and distinct. Secure: Both views correctly identified with some use of sources. Developing: One view well explained; the second underdeveloped. Emerging: Vague reference to 'for and against'.

practice_questions.text: 'Religious believers should always oppose both abortion and euthanasia.' Evaluate this statement, considering more than one point of view.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Argues that many traditions do oppose both (Catholic absolute prohibition; Islamic sovereignty of Allah; Buddhist first Precept), citing specific sources for each. Then argues that the picture is more nuanced: Jewish law permits abortion to save the mother; some Buddhist scholars allow euthanasia as compassion; even Christian denominations differ. Non-religious challenge: Dignity in Dying and Peter Singer. Clear, justified personal conclusion. Secure: Both sides addressed; some sources used; conclusion reached. Developing: One-sided or conclusion missing. Emerging: Simple opinion with no engagement with evidence.

practice_questions.text: Give two of the Five Pillars of Sunni Islam.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: Shahadah, Salat, Zakat, Sawm, Hajj.

practice_questions.text: What is wudu?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: The ritual washing performed before Islamic prayer, involving washing the hands, mouth, nose, face, arms, head, and feet in a set order, to purify the person before standing before Allah. Developing: Washing before prayer in Islam.

practice_questions.text: Describe how and why Muslims observe Sawm during Ramadan.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Accurate description (abstaining from food, drink, smoking, sexual relations from dawn to sunset; suhoor, iftar); explanations of purpose (self-discipline, empathy with the poor, gratitude, spiritual focus, Ramadan as month of Qur'an revelation, Qur'an 2:183). Secure: Description with one clear reason. Developing: Partial description, little explanation. Emerging: Vague reference to fasting in Ramadan.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the Hajj demonstrates the unity and equality of the Muslim community.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Ihram garments remove distinctions; millions of pilgrims from every nation united in identical rituals; tawaf, Arafah, and animal sacrifice all performed together; the ummah made visible. Secure: Two clear ways Hajj expresses equality/unity. Developing: One way described without full explanation. Emerging: Vague mention of Muslims going to Mecca.

practice_questions.text: Explain two Muslim beliefs about Salat (prayer) and its importance in Muslim life.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed beliefs each with a named source. e.g. (1) Salat is a direct command from Allah — Qur'an 29:45 says prayer restrains from shameful deeds, linking worship to moral formation; (2) Salat structures the entire day around submission to Allah — the five times are not arbitrary but connect the worshipper to the divine rhythm of the day. Secure: Two beliefs with at least one source cited and interpreted. Developing: Two beliefs briefly stated; sources absent. Emerging: One belief only.

practice_questions.text: 'The Hajj is the most important of the Five Pillars.' Evaluate this statement, referring to Islamic teachings and non-religious perspectives.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Structured argument. Agree: Hajj is the physical journey that unites the global ummah; its scale and intensity are unmatched; ihram symbolises equality before Allah; it is commanded for all who are able. Disagree: Salat happens five times every day — its daily role in shaping a Muslim's conscience (Qur'an 29:45) arguably makes it more foundational; Shahadah is the gateway to the entire faith; Sawm (Qur'an 2:183) develops taqwa that sustains all other pillars; Hajj is a once-in-a-lifetime obligation for many, whereas Salat is daily. Non-religious view: all five are cultural traditions; what matters is ethical behaviour in community, which doesn't require pilgrimage. Clear justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides with at least two sources; conclusion present. Developing: One-sided or weak sources. Emerging: Simple assertion.

practice_questions.text: Give two religious reasons why a person might refuse to fight in a war.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two of: belief in ahimsa / non-violence; the teaching that God is present in all people (Quaker); metta / compassion for all living beings (Buddhist); the first of the Five Precepts prohibits taking life; Islam permits only defensive war under strict conditions; Jewish preference for peace and preservation of life. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: What is meant by a 'conscientious objector'?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear definition stating that a conscientious objector is a person who refuses to serve in the armed forces on grounds of moral or religious belief.
Secure: A broadly accurate definition with minor gaps.
Developing: Partial definition.
Emerging: Vague or incorrect.

practice_questions.text: Describe what teshuvah means in Judaism and explain why Yom Kippur is important in relation to forgiveness.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate description of teshuvah (repentance/return — genuine regret, confession, reparation, change of behaviour) with a clear explanation that on Yom Kippur Jews collectively seek forgiveness from God and from those they have wronged, making it the most solemn day in the Jewish year.
Secure: Accurate description of teshuvah and Yom Kippur with some development.
Developing: One element described with limited detail.
Emerging: Very basic reference. [5 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two religious beliefs about forgiveness.
For each belief, refer to a source of wisdom or authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two developed beliefs from two traditions, each with a named and interpreted source (e.g. Matthew 18:21–22 for Christianity; GGS 866 for Sikhism or Qur'an 42:40 for Islam). Each belief developed with explanation of why it matters theologically.
Secure: Two beliefs with sources, one or both developed.
Developing: One belief with source or two beliefs without adequate sources.
Emerging: Simple points only. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two contrasting religious views on pacifism.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two genuinely contrasting views (e.g. Quaker absolute pacifism vs. Islamic permission of defensive war; Buddhist ahimsa vs. Sikh sant-sipahi tradition) both developed with sources and clear explanation of the contrast.
Secure: Two contrasting views, both developed though contrast may not be fully analysed.
Developing: Two views noted but contrast unclear.
Emerging: One view or very limited content. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Religious believers should always forgive those who wrong them.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to religious teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Christian teaching (Matthew 18:21–22; Lord's Prayer) demands unlimited forgiveness.
• Buddhism teaches metta and the Dhammapada lesson that hatred cannot end hatred.
• Islam presents forgiveness as superior to retaliation (Qur'an 42:40).

Arguments against:
• Jewish teshuvah requires genuine repentance first — forgiveness is not unconditional.
• The wronged party may need justice before forgiveness is appropriate or healing.
• Humanists note forgiveness is psychologically beneficial but should not require victims to suppress their experience of harm.

Mastering: Balanced, sophisticated argument; multiple traditions engaged; non-religious view included; clear justified conclusion.
Secure: Two developed viewpoints with sources; conclusion present.
Developing: Some argument but limited balance or weak conclusion.
Emerging: One-sided or minimal content. [15 marks + SPaG 5%]

practice_questions.text: Give two religious teachings that oppose racial discrimination.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: Galatians 3:27-29 (neither Jew nor Gentile in Christ) / Acts 10:34-35 (God does not show favouritism) / Qur'an 49:13 (diversity as God's design) / Guru Granth Sahib ang 349 (no high or low in God's creation) / Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 (no one's ancestor is greater). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: What is the difference between prejudice and discrimination?
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for: prejudice is an unfair preconceived attitude or opinion [1 mark]; discrimination is acting on that prejudice by treating someone unequally or unjustly [1 mark]. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how Martin Luther King Jr. used his Christian faith to oppose racial discrimination.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Detailed description of King as a Baptist minister; his use of agape (unconditional love) and the 'beloved community'; the Letter from Birmingham Jail (1963) — arguing unjust laws need not be obeyed using Augustine and Aquinas; his non-violent direct action; how his theology motivated his activism.
Secure: Two or more features described with some explanation of the religious connection.
Developing: One feature described with limited religious connection.
Emerging: Simple statement that King was Christian and opposed racism. [5 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain how two different religious traditions teach that racial discrimination is wrong.
Refer to sources of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two traditions clearly distinguished, each with a named source and interpretation. E.g. Christianity: Acts 10:34-35 (God does not show favouritism) + Catholic Catechism 1934-1938 (racial discrimination contrary to God's design); Islam: Qur'an 49:13 (diversity as God's plan so people might know one another) + Qur'an 5:8 (stand firmly for justice without allowing hatred to cause injustice). Each developed with explanation.
Secure: Two traditions with named sources; adequate explanation.
Developing: Two traditions; one developed.
Emerging: One tradition, limited development. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two contrasting Hindu attitudes towards caste and racial equality.
Refer to sources of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Traditional view — varna system (Rig Veda 10:90 Purusha Sukta) has been used to justify hierarchical social roles; contrasting view — reform movements (Gandhi challenging untouchability; Ramakrishna Mission; ISKCON) argue that the universal presence of Brahman in all people contradicts any hierarchy based on birth. Both views developed with named sources.
Secure: Two contrasting views each with a source; clear explanation.
Developing: Two views; limited source use.
Emerging: One view described. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Religion is the most important reason why people work against racial discrimination.'
Evaluate this statement, considering more than one point of view. Refer to religion and belief in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support: Martin Luther King grounded civil rights work explicitly in Christian agape and the beloved community; Islamic ummah transcends racial boundaries (Qur'an 49:13); Sikh Khalsa was founded partly to protect the oppressed; Jewish tikkun olam and HIAS work motivated by religious memory of persecution; Gandhi and Ambedkar both drew on religious frameworks.
Arguments against: Amnesty International and Humanists UK work against racism without religious grounding, using reason and empathy; secular laws (UK Equality Act 2010) provide legal protection regardless of religion; some discrimination has been committed by religious groups (caste in Hinduism, 969 Movement); science and human rights law offer non-religious arguments for equality.
Conclusion: Religion has been enormously important historically but is not the only motivation; a justified conclusion should weigh both religious and secular sources.
Mastering: Sustained argument, both sides, named sources, justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides with sources; conclusion reached.
Developing: One side stronger; limited sources.
Emerging: One-sided; few sources. [15 marks + 6 SPaG]

practice_questions.text: Give two reasons why some religious traditions oppose the use of artificial contraception.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of any two: sex must remain open to new life / procreation (Natural Law, Catholic); artificial contraception violates the God-given link between sex and new life (Humanae Vitae); 'be fruitful and multiply' is a divine command (Jewish); life is sacred and preventing conception may violate this (various traditions). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: What is meant by 'Natural Law' in Christian ethics?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear definition that Natural Law is the ethical theory associated with Aquinas that moral rules can be derived from the natural purposes God has built into human nature, discernible by reason.
Secure: Broadly accurate definition with minor gaps.
Developing: Partial definition.
Emerging: Vague or incorrect.

practice_questions.text: Describe Catholic teaching on sex and contraception, referring to at least one source of authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate description of Natural Law / Aquinas's second primary precept (reproduction); the teaching of Humanae Vitae (1968, Pope Paul VI) that each sexual act must be open to new life; CCC 2362–2363 on sexual love within marriage. At least one source named and explained.
Secure: Accurate description with one source named.
Developing: Basic description with limited source reference.
Emerging: Very little relevant content. [5 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two religious beliefs about sex outside marriage.
In your answer, refer to a source of wisdom or authority for each belief.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two developed beliefs from two traditions, each with a named and interpreted source (e.g. Qur'an 17:32 for Islam; GGS 335 for Sikhism; Third Precept / Triratna interpretation for Buddhism). Full development of what the source teaches.
Secure: Two beliefs with sources, one or both developed.
Developing: One developed belief with source, or two without sources.
Emerging: Simple points only. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain two contrasting religious views on contraception.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two genuinely contrasting views (e.g. Catholic opposition grounded in Humanae Vitae vs. Anglican acceptance since Lambeth 1930; or Orthodox Jewish caution vs. Reform Jewish support for reproductive autonomy). Both views developed with sources; contrast clearly drawn.
Secure: Two contrasting views developed, contrast noted.
Developing: Two views without genuine contrast.
Emerging: One view or very limited development. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Religious attitudes towards sexual ethics are outdated and harmful.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to religious teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Restrictions on contraception (Humanae Vitae) are criticised for contributing to population pressure and limiting women's reproductive autonomy.
• The Jewish get system has been criticised for leaving some women unable to remarry in Orthodox law.
• Some Islamic and traditional Christian views on gender roles are seen by critics as limiting women's equality.
• Humanists argue individuals should have autonomy over their own sexual and reproductive lives.

Arguments against:
• Catholic Natural Law provides a coherent ethical framework grounding sex in human nature and dignity, not arbitrary rules.
• Religious teachings on fidelity and commitment protect individuals and families from the harms of casual or exploitative relationships.
• Many religious traditions have engaged seriously with changing social contexts — e.g. Lambeth 1930 (Anglican contraception), Reform Judaism on divorce, Triratna on same-sex relationships.
• Many believers find religious sexual ethics liberating rather than restrictive, providing a framework of meaning within which relationships flourish.

Mastering: Sophisticated, balanced evaluation; multiple traditions engaged; Humanist view included; clear justified personal conclusion.
Secure: Two developed viewpoints with references; conclusion present.
Developing: Some argument; limited balance or weak conclusion.
Emerging: One-sided or minimal. [15 marks. Spelling, punctuation and grammar carry extra marks on specified extended-writing questions.]

practice_questions.text: Give two literary forms found in the Bible.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two correct forms: poetry; narrative/history; law; parable; prophecy; apocalyptic; letter/epistle; wisdom writing. Two marks maximum.

practice_questions.text: What does the term 'inspiration' mean in relation to the Bible?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: The process by which God guided human authors to write what he wished to communicate, without overriding their human personalities, cultures or literary forms — so that Scripture is truly the Word of God expressed through human words. Secure: God guided human authors to write Scripture. Developing: The Bible is God's word. Emerging: The Bible is inspired.

practice_questions.text: Describe what the Creation of Adam by Michelangelo communicates about Catholic beliefs.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Detailed description of the fresco — God reaching towards Adam, the gap between fingertips, what this expresses theologically (imago Dei from Genesis 1:26–27, God as personal and loving, human life as divine gift). Reference to where the painting is housed (Sistine Chapel) and its catechetical function — teaching doctrine visually. Secure: Two features of the painting with one theological significance explained. Developing: Basic description with one point about meaning. Emerging: Simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Explain the influence of the Catholic understanding of literary forms on how Catholics read Genesis.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains that recognising literary forms means Genesis 1 is read as a theological poem (not a science textbook); the seven-day structure is a liturgical framework; the truth communicated is about God as Creator, human dignity (imago Dei) and the Fall — not the physical mechanism of creation. Influences Catholic acceptance of theistic evolution. Reference to Dei Verbum or the Catechism. Secure: Two developed points of influence. Developing: One developed point. Emerging: Simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain two different Christian views on the Genesis accounts of creation. Refer to scripture or Church teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two contrasting views, each developed with a source. View 1: Literalist — Genesis 1 is a straightforward historical record; the world was created in six twenty-four-hour days; Scripture must be taken at face value on all matters; basis in a reading of Genesis 1:1–2:3 as historical narrative. View 2: Theistic evolution — God created through natural processes; Catholics (including Pope John Paul II's 1996 Pontifical Academy address) affirm evolution is compatible with faith provided the rational soul is directly created by God; Genesis is theological, not scientific. Each view explained with reasoning and source. Secure: Two views with one source. Developing: One view developed. Emerging: Simple statement of one view.

practice_questions.text: 'Sacred art is more important than Scripture for understanding Catholic beliefs.' Evaluate this statement from a Catholic perspective, considering more than one point of view.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: Sacred art (e.g. Creation of Adam, San Clemente mosaic) communicates complex doctrine visually and accessibly — before widespread literacy, art was the primary means by which ordinary Catholics learned theology. Art can make abstract doctrines (imago Dei, Trinity, salvation) emotionally vivid. Art is less open to misinterpretation through language barriers. Arguments against: Scripture is the Word of God — divinely inspired, authoritative and the foundation of all Catholic doctrine. The Catechism, Dei Verbum and tradition all give Scripture primacy as a source of revelation. Art interprets Scripture; it cannot replace it. Theological meaning in art depends on the viewer knowing the Scriptural narrative behind it. Non-religious view: Both Scripture and art are human creations reflecting human culture and experience; neither is uniquely authoritative. Conclusion: A strong answer will argue that art and Scripture are complementary rather than competing — art embodies and extends Scriptural truth. Most Catholics would hold Scripture as primary while valuing art as a vital mode of theological expression. Mastering: Sustained argument, sources named and interpreted, justified conclusion. Secure: Two sides with one source. Developing: One side. Emerging: Simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Give two titles used for Jesus Christ in the Nicene Creed.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from the Nicene Creed: 'Lord'; 'true God from true God'; 'begotten, not made'; 'consubstantial with the Father'; 'the Only Begotten Son of God'. Two marks maximum.

practice_questions.text: What does the term 'kenosis' mean in relation to the Incarnation?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: The self-emptying of the Son of God in taking on human nature, described in Philippians 2:5–11, where Christ empties himself by taking the form of a servant — an act of divine humility and love. Secure: Christ emptying himself to become human. Developing: Jesus giving up his power to become human. Emerging: When Jesus became human.

practice_questions.text: Describe Augustine's analogy of the Trinity as lover, beloved and love in De Trinitate 8.10.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Accurate description of the analogy — Augustine identifies a Trinitarian structure in love: the lover (Father), the beloved (Son) and the love that flows between them (Holy Spirit); love is not a feeling but a person; the analogy works because humans are made in God's image (imago Dei), so something of the Trinity's inner life is reflected in human experience; Augustine acknowledges the analogy's limits. Secure: Two features of the analogy with one theological point. Developing: Basic description of the three terms. Emerging: Simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Explain the influence of the doctrine of the Incarnation on Catholic moral teaching.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains that the Incarnation means God took on human nature — giving human bodily existence dignity and sanctity; Jesus's moral teaching in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7) therefore carries divine authority; the Incarnation shows Natural Law truths embodied in a human life; it gives Catholic moral theology a respect for bodily and material life (against dualism); connects to kenosis hymn (Philippians 2:5–11) — the willingness of the Son to suffer shows that suffering is not beneath God. Secure: Two developed points. Developing: One developed point. Emerging: Simple statement.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which the Nicene Creed expresses Catholic beliefs about God.
Refer to a source of Catholic teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed ways with sources. Way 1: The Creed affirms the Son is 'true God from true God, begotten not made, consubstantial with the Father' — answering the Arian heresy that the Son was a created being; supported by John 1:1 ('the Word was God') and John 1:14. Way 2: The Creed affirms the Holy Spirit as 'the Lord, the giver of life' — a full divine person; Galatians 5:22–23 lists the Spirit's fruits (love, joy, peace etc.) as evidence of the Spirit's active presence in believers. Each way with source and theological significance. Secure: Two ways with one source. Developing: One developed way. Emerging: Simple statement.

practice_questions.text:
'The Incarnation makes no sense — a perfect God would never become human.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to Catholic teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: The statement reflects a philosophical objection — an infinite, perfect, unchanging God cannot take on finite, limited, suffering human form without contradiction. The Incarnation seems to demean the divine. Non-religious philosophers argue the concept is logically incoherent (how can one person be both all-knowing and limited in knowledge?). Arguments against: Catholic theology argues the Incarnation is the supreme expression of divine love — the kenosis hymn (Philippians 2:5–11) presents God's self-emptying not as a contradiction but as the fullness of love. John 1:14 ('the Word became flesh') is the bedrock. Athanasius argued: 'God became man so that man might become God' — the Incarnation is the means of human salvation and deification. Augustine's De Trinitate shows God is inherently relational (Trinity); becoming human is an extension of relational love. Salvifici Doloris shows the Incarnate God entering human suffering transforms it from within. Non-religious view: Humanists see Jesus as a great moral teacher whose example is valuable without requiring divine status — the Incarnation doctrine adds theological complexity unnecessary for ethical inspiration. Conclusion: A strong answer will argue the Incarnation is the theological heart of Catholic Christianity — without it, Christ's moral teaching and his redemptive suffering lose their authority and power. Whether it 'makes sense' depends on prior commitments about what God can and cannot do. Mastering: Sustained argument, sources, conclusion. Secure: Two sides, one source. Developing: One side. Emerging: Simple view.

practice_questions.text: Give two Christian beliefs about the Incarnation.
practice_questions.marks: Award one mark per accurate belief, up to two marks. Examples: the eternal Son of God took on human flesh; Jesus was both fully divine and fully human; the Incarnation is described in John 1:14 ('the Word became flesh'). StudyVault rubric: Mastering — two precise beliefs using accurate theological language. Emerging — one vague point.

practice_questions.text: What does the term 'atonement' mean in Christianity?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a precise two-point definition — atonement is the reconciliation between God and humanity brought about through the death of Jesus Christ, restoring the relationship broken by sin. Secure: accurate one-sentence definition. Emerging: a vague reference to Jesus dying for sins.

practice_questions.text: Describe Christian teaching about the resurrection of Jesus.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5): detailed description including the empty tomb (John 20:1-21), appearances to Mary Magdalene and the disciples, showing of wounds, relevance to Christian hope of eternal life, and connection to atonement. Secure (3-4): clear account of key events with some significance explained. Developing (2): basic account of the empty tomb. Emerging (1): a simple statement that Jesus rose from the dead.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which the crucifixion of Jesus influences Christian belief today.
Refer to a source of Christian teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7-8): two well-developed beliefs each linked to scripture or theological teaching, with explanation of significance. Examples: (1) The cross shows the depth of divine love — John 3:16 teaches that God gave his Son so believers can have eternal life; this motivates Christians to love and serve others sacrificially. (2) Jesus' death achieved atonement — the torn Temple curtain (Mark 15:38) symbolises that all people now have direct access to God; Christians understand this as forgiveness being available to everyone. Secure (5-6): two beliefs developed with some reference to teaching. Developing (3-4): one developed belief or two undeveloped points. Emerging (1-2): simple statements only.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which belief in the ascension of Jesus influences Christian practice.
Refer to a source of Christian teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7-8): two well-developed influences linked to Acts 1:9-11 or John 14:1-4. Examples: (1) Belief in the Ascension shapes Christian hope — Jesus promised to prepare a place in his Father's house (John 14:1-4); this motivates Christians to live according to his teachings in expectation of eternal life. (2) The Ascension set the scene for Pentecost — the disciples were told to wait for the Holy Spirit (Acts 1); Christians today believe the Spirit guides them, seen in prayer and worship. Secure (5-6): two beliefs with some development. Developing (3-4): limited development. Emerging (1-2): bare statements.

practice_questions.text: 'The resurrection of Jesus is the most important event in Christianity.' Evaluate this statement, considering more than one point of view.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: the Resurrection is the foundation of Christian faith (Paul argues without it faith is pointless, 1 Corinthians 15:14); it proves Jesus is the Son of God and that death is conquered; it gives Christians confidence in their own resurrection and eternal life; Easter is the most important festival in the Christian year. Arguments against: the Incarnation could be seen as equally central — without God becoming human (John 1:14) there could be no crucifixion or resurrection; the crucifixion (atonement) achieves the actual rescue from sin that salvation requires; the Ascension and sending of the Spirit are what make the ongoing Christian community possible. Conclusion: a justified personal view that weighs the events. Mastering (13-15): sustained argument, precise use of sources, clear conclusion. Secure (9-12): two sides developed with some source use. Developing (5-8): one side stronger, limited sources. Emerging (1-4): one-sided or descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Give two Catholic organisations that work for social justice.
practice_questions.marks: One mark per accurate organisation, up to two. Examples: CAFOD (Catholic Agency for Overseas Development), CARJ (Catholic Association for Racial Justice), St Vincent de Paul Society. Mastering: two named organisations with correct identification. Emerging: one vague reference to a charity.

practice_questions.text: What does 'virtue ethics' mean in Catholic moral teaching?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: virtue ethics is an approach (developed by Aristotle and adopted by Aquinas) that focuses on cultivating good character traits — virtues — so that a person habitually acts rightly; it asks 'what kind of person should I be?' rather than simply 'what should I do?' Secure: accurate one-sentence definition. Emerging: 'doing good things' without further explanation.

practice_questions.text: Describe the structure and significance of the Mass for Catholics.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5): detailed description including both parts (Liturgy of the Word and Liturgy of the Eucharist), transubstantiation (bread and wine become body and blood of Christ), the last supper institution (1 Corinthians 11:23-26), the parish/diocese structure, and 'living the Mass' as social action. Secure (3-4): clear account of key elements with some significance. Developing (2): basic account of going to church and receiving communion. Emerging (1): simple statement that Catholics attend Mass.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Catholic beliefs about the Sacrament of Reconciliation.
Refer to a source of Catholic teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7-8): two well-developed beliefs, each linked to scripture or Church teaching. Examples: (1) Reconciliation restores the relationship with God after serious sin — Catholics believe Jesus gave authority to forgive sins to his apostles (John 20:22-23); the priest acting 'in persona Christi' pronounces absolution, which Catholics believe is genuine divine forgiveness. (2) Reconciliation is connected to virtue growth — regular confession develops the virtues of humility and honesty; Jesus' teaching on unlimited forgiveness (Matthew 18:21-22) and the Lord's Prayer link receiving God's forgiveness to forgiving others, making reconciliation a moral as well as sacramental practice. Secure (5-6): two beliefs with development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two undeveloped. Emerging (1-2): simple statements.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which the teaching of 'Gaudium et Spes' influences Catholic social action today.
Refer to a source of Catholic teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7-8): two well-developed ways linked to Gaudium et Spes 78 and/or 29. Examples: (1) GS 78 calls Catholics to build peace through justice; this motivates CAFOD's overseas development work — tackling the root causes of poverty is seen as a form of peacebuilding demanded by the Gospel. (2) GS 29 affirms the fundamental equality of all humans; this underpins CARJ's work against racial discrimination within the Church and society — discrimination contradicts the Catholic teaching that all are made in the image of God. Pope Francis' Evangelii Gaudium also calls Catholics to serve the poor as an extension of 'living the Mass'. Secure (5-6): two ways with development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two undeveloped. Emerging (1-2): vague reference to charity work.

practice_questions.text:
'Virtue ethics is more useful than divine command ethics for Catholics making moral decisions.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Catholic teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: virtue ethics focuses on becoming a good person, not just following rules, which aligns with Jesus' teaching that moral goodness flows from the heart (Matthew 5-7, Sermon on the Mount); Aquinas's adoption of Aristotle shows its deep roots in Catholic intellectual tradition; virtue ethics handles complex situations not covered by simple rules; it encourages ongoing growth in character rather than mere rule compliance. Arguments against: divine command ethics provides clear, God-given moral guidance that does not shift with circumstances; the Ten Commandments and the Catechism give Catholics authoritative moral rules directly from God; relativist approaches using virtue judgement risk subjective rationalisation of wrong actions; the Catechism's absolute prohibitions (e.g. on abortion, CCC 2270) reflect the absolutist strand, which many Catholics see as essential. Conclusion: justified personal view noting that Catholic tradition actually uses both in complementary ways. Mastering (13-15): sustained argument, precise sources, clear conclusion. Secure (9-12): two sides. Developing (5-8): one-sided. Emerging (1-4): descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Give two features of puja in a Hindu mandir.

practice_questions.text: What is 'bhakti' in Hinduism?
practice_questions.marks: Two marks for: devotional love directed towards a personal deity, understood as one of the spiritual paths to liberation (moksha). One mark for: 'devotion' or 'love for God' without further explanation.

practice_questions.text: Describe the features and significance of the Hindu sacred thread ceremony (Upanayana).

practice_questions.text: Explain how pilgrimage to Varanasi influences Hindu beliefs and practice.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two beliefs about puja in Hinduism.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Belief 1: Puja is an act of selfless devotion — the Bhagavad Gita (3:19) teaches action performed as duty, without selfish attachment, is spiritually purifying. Belief 2: The murti is not an idol but the living presence of God — Hindus treat the murti as the deity themselves. Could also develop bhakti as a path to moksha. Emerging: One belief with little development.

practice_questions.text:
'For Hindus, the most important rite of passage is cremation, not the sacred thread ceremony.'
Evaluate this statement.

Disagrees: the Upanayana marks second birth into religious life — it structures the whole of adult Hindu practice; for male Hindus of the top three varnas it was historically the gateway to spiritual study. Both are part of the samskaras framework. Non-religious view: secular perspectives might argue the most important transition is birth (because it initiates life). Justified conclusion with personal stance. Secure: Two developed sides with at least one source; some evaluation. Developing: Some points on both sides, limited evaluation. Emerging: Descriptive, one-sided.

practice_questions.text: Give two features of a synagogue interior.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the Shema expresses Jewish beliefs about God.

practice_questions.text: What does 'redemption' mean in Catholic theology?
practice_questions.marks:

Emerging: Something to do with Jesus.

practice_questions.text: Describe the significance of the altar and font in a Catholic church.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A detailed description covering: the altar is the focal point of the church at which the Eucharist (Mass) is celebrated; it symbolises both the table of the Last Supper and the altar of sacrifice — the Mass makes present the once-for-all sacrifice of Calvary; Vatican II (Lumen Gentium 11) called the Eucharist the 'source and summit of the Christian life'; the font is placed near the entrance to symbolise that baptism is the gateway into the Church and into salvation; through baptism a person first shares in the death and resurrection of Christ.
Secure: A clear description with two theological meanings.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the Church's teaching on salvation influences Catholic attitudes towards mission and evangelisation.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A developed explanation covering: if salvation comes through Christ and his Church (John 14:6; CCC 846–848), then sharing the Gospel is an act of love — bringing people the means of salvation; the Great Commission (Matthew 28:18–20) mandates the Church to make disciples of all nations; Catholic organisations such as Missio carry out this mission globally; at the same time, CCC 846–848 acknowledges that God can save those outside the Church, which prevents aggressive exclusivism; the goal is sharing the gift of faith, not condemning the unbaptised.

Developing: One influence without theological grounding.
Emerging: Brief mention of mission.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Catholic beliefs about the nature of the Church.
Refer to a source of Catholic teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two fully developed beliefs with named sources. Belief 1 might be that the Church is the Body of Christ (1 Corinthians 12; CCC 787–796): Christ is the head, all the baptised are members with different gifts; when one member suffers, all suffer; the Church's unity is organic, not merely institutional. Belief 2 might be that the Church is 'one, holy, catholic and apostolic' (the four marks, Nicene Creed; CCC 811–870): its unity under one Lord, its call to holiness, its universality across cultures, and its continuity with the apostles through apostolic succession, make it uniquely the Church of Christ.
Secure: Two beliefs with named sources.
Developing: One belief well explained, second superficial.
Emerging: One brief point.

practice_questions.text:
'The Catholic Church's teaching that salvation comes only through Christ is incompatible with a God of unconditional love.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Catholic teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• If God genuinely wills the salvation of all (1 Timothy 2:4) but salvation is available only to those who explicitly believe in Christ, then billions of people who lived before Christ or who have never encountered Christianity are excluded through no fault of their own — which seems incompatible with unconditional love.
• From a Humanist or pluralist perspective, the idea that only one religion has the key to salvation is exclusivist and historically has been used to justify harmful missionary activity.
• The statement 'no one comes to the Father except through me' (John 14:6) can appear to condemn the majority of humanity.

Arguments against:
• The Catechism (CCC 846–848) explicitly teaches that God is 'not bound' to his sacraments and can save those who, through no fault of their own, have not encountered the explicit Gospel — so exclusion is not automatic.
• The Catholic tradition holds that all salvation comes through Christ, but that he can work through ways known only to God — meaning the salvation of non-Christians is possible without formal membership of the Church.
• God's unconditional love is expressed in the freedom given to human beings to accept or reject grace; hell is chosen, not imposed.
• Pope Francis's Evangelii Gaudium (2013) and his wider teaching on God's universal mercy are part of the ordinary Magisterium's ongoing affirmation that divine love is genuinely unlimited in its offer.

Conclusion: A justified conclusion should assess whether the exclusivity of Christ as mediator is compatible with the universality of God's saving will, concluding that the Catholic position attempts to hold both together — through Christ all are potentially saved, but the scope is unlimited.

Mastering: Sophisticated argument with named sources and clear justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides with some sources and a conclusion.
Developing: One-sided or conclusion missing.
Emerging: Simple statements without reasoning.

practice_questions.marks: Award one mark for each correct example, up to two. Acceptable answers include: papal encyclical (e.g. Evangelium Vitae, Laudato Si') / the Catechism of the Catholic Church / a bishop's pastoral letter / an apostolic exhortation / the Bishops' Conference of England and Wales statement on a moral issue.

practice_questions.text: What is the Paschal Candle?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A large candle blessed and lit at the Easter Vigil, inscribed with the year, Alpha and Omega, and five grains of incense; it symbolises the risen Christ as the light of the world and is used at baptisms and funerals throughout the year.
Secure: A large candle lit at Easter, used at Catholic funerals and baptisms to symbolise the risen Christ.
Developing: A candle used at Catholic ceremonies.
Emerging: A religious object used in church.

practice_questions.text: Describe the significance of the Paschal Candle at a Catholic funeral.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A detailed description covering: the Paschal Candle is first lit at the Easter Vigil to represent the risen Christ; its presence at a funeral connects the deceased to the paschal mystery (Christ's dying and rising); it symbolises the belief that the deceased has 'passed over' from death to life, just as Christ did; the same candle is used at baptism, linking the beginning and end of a Catholic's sacramental life; the symbols inscribed on it (Alpha and Omega, five wounds of Christ, the year) reinforce its theological meaning.
Secure: A clear description with at least two pieces of theological meaning.
Developing: Description of what the candle looks like without explaining its significance.
Emerging: Vague reference to a candle at a funeral.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the Second Vatican Council has influenced Catholic teaching on human dignity and the afterlife.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A developed explanation covering: Vatican II (1962–65) produced Gaudium et Spes, which affirmed that death is the moment when the 'riddle of human existence' becomes most acute, and that the resurrection answers it; the council reformed the funeral rite to emphasise resurrection hope; Lumen Gentium re-centred the Church as 'the people of God' sharing in the paschal mystery; post-council encyclicals (Evangelium Vitae 65 on euthanasia, Salvifici Doloris on suffering) continued this development.
Secure: Two or more clear influences explained with reference to named documents.
Developing: One influence described without reference to specific documents.
Emerging: Brief mention of Vatican II without substance.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Catholic beliefs about the role of the Magisterium as a source of authority.
Refer to a source of Catholic teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two fully developed beliefs with sources. Belief 1 might be that the ordinary Magisterium (encyclicals, Catechism, bishops' pastoral letters) provides authoritative but non-infallible teaching on faith and morals, which Catholics are to adhere to with 'religious assent' (CCC 892). Belief 2 might be that the extraordinary Magisterium (ex cathedra pronouncements, ecumenical councils such as Vatican II) is infallible, guided by the Holy Spirit in fulfilment of Christ's promise to Peter (Matthew 16:18). Only two papal dogmas have been defined ex cathedra: the Immaculate Conception (1854) and the Assumption of Mary (1950).
Secure: Two beliefs explained with sources.
Developing: One belief well explained; the second superficial.
Emerging: One brief point.

practice_questions.text:
'Sacred art and music such as the Requiem are essential for Catholic funeral worship.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Catholic teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Sacred music such as Fauré's Requiem (completed 1890) expresses the theology of resurrection hope in a way that spoken words cannot — the consoling, serene character of the In Paradisum and Lux Aeterna communicates confidence in God's mercy.
• The Paschal Candle, white pall, holy water and incense at Catholic funerals are theological statements as much as ritual actions: they proclaim resurrection faith through symbol.
• Vatican II's Sacrosanctum Concilium affirmed the importance of the arts in Catholic worship as a form of communication accessible to all believers regardless of education.
• Early Christian sarcophagi show that using art to express resurrection faith is as old as Christianity itself.

Arguments against:
• A minimalist or evangelical view might argue that heartfelt prayer and scripture are sufficient — elaborate ritual and art may distract from the essentials of faith.
• From a Humanist perspective, such rituals are comforting fictions that obscure the reality of death as the end of personal existence.
• Some Catholic communities in Britain opt for simple funeral Masses without elaborate music, arguing that prayerful simplicity is equally valid.

Conclusion: A justified conclusion should weigh the theological value of sacred art as a vehicle for doctrine against the argument that simpler forms of worship are equally effective.

Mastering: Sophisticated argument with named sources and justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides with some sources and a conclusion.
Developing: One-sided or conclusion missing.
Emerging: Simple statements without reasoning.

practice_questions.text:
'Meditation is the most important Buddhist practice.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Buddhist teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Dhammapada 282 teaches that wisdom arises through meditation and is lost without it — placing meditation at the centre of the path to liberation.
• Samatha develops the mental stability needed for insight; vipassana directly reveals the Three Marks, the proximate cause of enlightenment.
• The Eightfold Path includes Right Mindfulness and Right Concentration (samadhi section), showing meditation is structurally central.
• The Sangha's communal practice often centres on meditation retreats as the context for deepening wisdom.
Arguments against:
• The Eightfold Path has three sections (wisdom, morality, meditation) — morality (sila) could be considered equally fundamental because it supports meditation.
• The Five Precepts are the primary ethical framework and are required before meditation can be fruitful.
• Taking refuge in the Three Jewels — particularly the Sangha community — may be considered the most foundational practice because it embeds the individual in the conditions for practice.
• Non-religious view: mindfulness is valued in secular psychology for wellbeing, independently of Buddhist doctrine.
Conclusion: Justified personal judgement.
Mastering: Sustained two-sided argument, sources from the dhamma, non-religious view, clear conclusion.
Secure: Both sides with one source, conclusion.
Developing: One side stronger, limited sources.
Emerging: One-sided, no conclusion.

practice_questions.text:
'The existence of suffering proves that God does not exist.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to religious teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• The problem of evil is a strong philosophical challenge: a good, all-powerful God should prevent suffering.
• Humanists / atheists (e.g. Richard Dawkins) argue suffering is better explained by evolution than by God's plan.
• Extreme suffering (e.g. the Holocaust) seems impossible to justify if God is both powerful and loving.

Arguments against:
• Augustinian theodicy: evil resulted from free will, not God's design.
• Irenaean soul-making: suffering enables moral and spiritual growth.
• Islamic teaching: hardship is a test and patient endurance (sabr) is spiritually meritorious.
• Buddhist/Hindu explanations: suffering arises from karma and craving, not from God's failure.

Mastering: Sophisticated, balanced argument; multiple traditions engaged; Humanist view included; clear, justified personal conclusion.
Secure: Two developed viewpoints with references; conclusion present.
Developing: Some argument; limited balance or weak conclusion.
Emerging: One-sided or minimal. [15 marks + SPaG 5%]

Bhagavad Gita 2:13 — the soul moves from body to body as a person moves from childhood to old age. Belief 2: Samsara involves suffering because of attachment to the material world — the goal is moksha, liberation from the cycle. Bhagavad Gita 2:22 — the soul casts off worn-out bodies like old clothes. Secure: Two beliefs explained with at least one textual reference. practice_questions.text:
'The Hindu caste system is incompatible with belief in the equality of all souls.'
Evaluate this statement.

practice_questions.text:
'Muslims who believe in al-Qadr cannot truly be held responsible for their actions.'
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sophisticated argument engaging with the tension between divine foreknowledge and human free will. Arguments in support: al-Qadr states God decrees all things; if God knows what will happen, human choice seems determined; some fatalist readings suggest events are 'written'. Arguments against: mainstream Muslim scholarship holds God's foreknowledge does not remove human free will; Muslims are taught to make genuine choices and will be judged on them (Yawm al-Qiyamah); the Qur'an commands right action repeatedly, implying humans can choose. Non-religious view: secular humanists affirm full human moral responsibility without reference to divine decree. Justified conclusion with personal stance. Secure: Two developed arguments (agree/disagree) with at least one source; some evaluation. Developing: Some points on both sides but little evaluation or no source.
