practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two of: Birthday of Guru Nanak / Birthday of Guru Gobind Singh / Martyrdom of Guru Arjan. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: What is the Lavan?
practice_questions.marks: The four wedding hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib (pages 773–774) recited and sung during the Sikh marriage ceremony, around which the couple circles four times. [2 marks — 1 for identification, 1 for explanation of significance]

practice_questions.text: Describe Sikh beliefs and teachings about equality.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Detailed account with two or more distinct points, specific reference to Guru Granth Sahib 349 or Khalsa founding, plus explanation of why equality matters in Sikh theology (God's light is in everyone; caste counts for nothing).
Secure: Two clear points (e.g. langar, caste condemnation) with some explanation of significance.
Developing: One or two points, mostly descriptive, limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple identification of one feature only.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the celebration of Vaisakhi influences the lives of Sikhs today.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two developed points showing influence (e.g. new Amrit initiations strengthen Khalsa identity; Nagar Kirtan processions bring community together and demonstrate faith publicly) each linked to the historical founding in 1699.
Secure: Two points with some explanation of influence.
Developing: One developed point or two simple points.
Emerging: Simple statement about Vaisakhi without explaining influence.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Sikh beliefs about the authority of the Guru Granth Sahib.
Refer to Sikh teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct beliefs each developed with a source of authority (e.g. treated as living Guru — chauri, Takht, ceremonial respect; eternal word of God replacing human Gurus — Guru Gobind Singh's declaration in 1708) and explained in terms of why it matters to Sikhs.
Secure: Two beliefs, each with reference to teaching and some development.
Developing: One well-developed belief or two briefly stated.
Emerging: One or two simple points, no source of authority.

practice_questions.text:
'The most important Sikh teaching is the equality of all people.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Sikh teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Guru Granth Sahib 349 teaches that God's light is in everyone and that caste counts for nothing — placing equality at the heart of revealed teaching.
• Practical institutions (langar, sangat, sewa) express equality in everyday Sikh life, making it more than abstract doctrine.
• Guru Gobind Singh's Khalsa abolished caste-based names, giving equality structural expression in Sikh identity.
• Non-religious view: humanist thinkers argue equality is the foundation of human dignity independently of any religious framework.
Arguments against:
• The authority of the Guru Granth Sahib as living Guru could be considered more fundamental — without this source of authority, equality teachings lose their divine grounding.
• Belief in one God (Waheguru) and the goal of mukti (union with God) might be argued as the theological foundation that makes all other teachings, including equality, possible.
• The Khalsa's five commitments (Five Ks) could be seen as the defining Sikh teaching because they involve active, visible commitment, not just belief.
Conclusion: A justified personal judgement weighing which teaching is most fundamental.
Mastering: Sustained two-sided argument with named sources, non-religious view included, clear justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides developed, at least one source, conclusion present.
Developing: One side stronger than other, limited sources.
Emerging: One-sided or no conclusion.

practice_questions.text: Give two of the Five Precepts followed by Buddhist lay practitioners.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two of: not harming any living being / not taking what is not given / avoiding sexual misconduct / avoiding false speech / not taking intoxicants. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: What is 'dana' in Buddhist practice?
practice_questions.marks: Dana means giving or generosity — the practice of making offerings (food, money, time) to monks, monasteries or the community, seen as generating merit and supporting the Sangha. [2 marks — 1 for identification, 1 for explanation]

practice_questions.text: Describe how Wesak is celebrated and what it means to Buddhists.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full account of Wesak as celebrating birth, enlightenment and death (Theravada), with at least two specific observances (offerings, lantern processions, dhamma teaching) and explanation of what this means (affirms that liberation is available to all).
Secure: Correct identification of Wesak with two features and some explanation.
Developing: Wesak identified with one or two features, limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple statement only.

practice_questions.text: Explain how following the Five Precepts influences the everyday lives of Buddhists.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two developed influences (e.g. first precept may lead to vegetarianism and career choices; fifth precept means avoiding alcohol in social contexts) with explanation of underlying Buddhist reasoning (sila supports samadhi and panna).
Secure: Two influences with some development.
Developing: One influence developed or two briefly stated.
Emerging: Simply names precepts without explaining influence.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two contrasting Buddhist views on how puja should be practised.
Refer to Buddhist teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two developed contrasting views (Theravada: single Buddha image, austere offerings, no petitionary prayer; Mahayana: multiple Buddhas/bodhisattvas, mudras, mantras, mandalas) each with doctrinal grounding and explanation of why the difference exists (different understandings of the path and of who can be a source of help).
Secure: Two contrasting views with some development and reference to teaching.
Developing: One view developed, one briefly stated.
Emerging: One view or simple comparison without development.

practice_questions.text:
'The Five Precepts are not relevant to modern life.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Buddhist teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Western consumer culture normalises alcohol, meat and sexual permissiveness, making the Five Precepts counter-cultural and difficult to maintain, especially the fifth precept.
• Triratna Buddhists living in Western culture acknowledge the challenge of adhering to the precepts in contemporary society.
• A secular Humanist might argue that ethical decisions should be contextual (situationist) rather than governed by a fixed list of rules.
Arguments against:
• Dhammapada 183 presents the ethical life as the foundation of Buddhist practice — not harming, cultivating good, purifying the mind are as relevant today as they were in the Buddha's time.
• The first precept (ahimsa) is particularly relevant in the modern world in relation to environmental harm, animal welfare and violence.
• The Five Precepts support mental clarity (sila enables samadhi), which is increasingly valued in secular mindfulness practice and evidence-based psychology.
• Triratna Buddhists argue that communal support and adapted practice make the precepts fully liveable in the contemporary West.
Conclusion: Justified personal judgement.
Mastering: Two sides developed, sources cited, non-religious view included, clear conclusion.
Secure: Both sides with reference, conclusion present.
Developing: One side stronger.
Emerging: One-sided, no conclusion.

practice_questions.text: Give two Christian beliefs about the afterlife.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two of: heaven (eternal life with God) / hell (separation from God) / purgatory (Catholic: state of purification) / resurrection of the body / judgement. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: What does 'akhirah' mean in Islamic belief?
practice_questions.marks: The Islamic belief in the afterlife — encompassing the period from death through the Day of Judgement to the eternal states of Jannah (paradise) and Jahannam (hell). [2 marks — 1 for identification, 1 for explanation]

practice_questions.text: Describe Sikh beliefs about life after death.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Samsara (cycle of rebirth), kamma, mukti (liberation and union with Waheguru), Guru Granth Sahib 13, God's grace (nadar), death as the soul's return to its source.
Secure: Two clear points (samsara, mukti) with some development.
Developing: One or two features briefly described.
Emerging: Simple statement only.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the teaching about samsara influences the beliefs of Hindus and Buddhists differently.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two developed comparisons — Hinduism affirms an eternal atman that transmigrates toward moksha; Buddhism denies a fixed self (anatta), with kamma transmitting not a soul but moral force toward nibbana. Both agree samsara is the problem; they differ on what is reborn and the goal.
Secure: Two points with some comparison and development.
Developing: One comparison developed.
Emerging: Simple statement about one tradition.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two contrasting beliefs about life after death.
Refer to sources of authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly contrasting beliefs from different traditions (e.g. Christian resurrection — John 11:24-27, 1 Corinthians 15:42-44 — versus Humanist 'death is the end'; or Islamic akhirah — Qur'an 46:33 — versus Buddhist nibbana without a fixed self) each developed with source and explanation of significance.
Secure: Two contrasting views, one source, some development.
Developing: Two views briefly stated.
Emerging: One view only.

practice_questions.text:
'Belief in an afterlife is essential to living a good life.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to religious teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Islamic teaching of akhirah (Day of Judgement) provides direct motivation for ethical living — actions have eternal consequences (Qur'an 46:33).
• Hindu karma and samsara mean that how one lives this life determines the conditions of future lives — belief in rebirth incentivises moral behaviour.
• Christian belief in heaven and hell (CCC 1033) provides a framework of ultimate justice: wrongdoers cannot escape divine judgement.
• Sikh mukti — achievable through devotion and righteous living — gives the ethical life a cosmic significance beyond mere social approval.
Arguments against:
• Humanists live ethically without any afterlife belief — moral behaviour is grounded in empathy, reason and care for others in this life alone.
• Buddhist Triratna tradition shows that afterlife beliefs can be interpreted psychologically (moment-to-moment rebirth) without undermining the ethical commitments of the Five Precepts.
• Jesus's teaching in the Gospels includes living ethically for the sake of the Kingdom of God, not merely to avoid hell.
• Many non-religious thinkers argue that upbringing, relationships and social norms shape how people behave far more than beliefs about an afterlife do.
Conclusion: Justified personal judgement.
Mastering: Two sides sustained, multiple traditions referenced, Humanist view included, clear justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides, one source, conclusion.
Developing: One side stronger.
Emerging: One-sided, no conclusion.

practice_questions.text: Give two Christian teachings about the use of wealth.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: Luke 16:19-31 (rich man and Lazarus — ignoring poverty has eternal consequences) / Luke 12:13-21 (parable of the rich fool — wealth is not ultimate security) / Mark 10:21-31 (sell everything and give to the poor) / Mark 12:41-44 (the widow's mite — sacrifice matters more than amount). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: What is the difference between absolute poverty and relative poverty?
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for: absolute poverty is lacking the basic necessities for survival (food, water, shelter) [1 mark]; relative poverty is having significantly less than the average standard of living in one's society [1 mark]. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how the Islamic teaching of zakat shapes Muslim attitudes towards wealth and poverty.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Detailed description of zakat as the third Pillar of Islam — an obligatory annual payment of 2.5% of accumulated wealth above the nisab; it purifies the rest of one's wealth; Qur'an 2:177 on righteousness including giving to those in need; Islamic Relief as a British charity embodying zakat in action; the distinction between zakat (obligation) and sadaqa (voluntary giving).
Secure: Two or more features described with explanation of why zakat matters theologically.
Developing: Basic description of zakat as obligatory giving with limited development.
Emerging: Simple statement that Muslims give to charity. [5 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain how two different religious traditions use charity organisations to respond to poverty.
Refer to sources of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two traditions clearly distinguished, each with a named charity and the religious teaching that motivates it. E.g. Christianity: CAFOD motivated by Catholic social teaching (preferential option for the poor) and Luke 16:19-31 (Dives and Lazarus — ignoring poverty has eternal consequences); Sikhism: Khalsa Aid motivated by sewa (selfless service as worship) and Guru Granth Sahib angs 42 and 1246. Each developed with explanation of the connection between teaching and action.
Secure: Two traditions with named charities and sources; adequate explanation.
Developing: Two traditions; one developed.
Emerging: One tradition; limited development. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two contrasting religious attitudes towards the acquisition of wealth.
Refer to sources of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: View 1 — some traditions are cautious about wealth (e.g. Mark 10:21-31 'sell everything and give to the poor'; Buddhist tanha/attachment as root of suffering; Right Livelihood limits how wealth may be earned). View 2 — other traditions accept wealth within limits (e.g. Hindu artha as a legitimate aim of life within dharma; Islamic teaching that wealth is a gift from God when shared through zakat). Both views developed with named sources.
Secure: Two contrasting views each with a source; clear explanation.
Developing: Two views; limited source use.
Emerging: One view described. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Religious people have a greater duty than non-religious people to help those living in poverty.'
Evaluate this statement, considering more than one point of view. Refer to religion and belief in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support: Zakat is a religious obligation — Muslims are commanded to give regardless of personal desire; Christian Aid and CAFOD are motivated by specific theological imperatives (Luke 16:19-31; Catholic preferential option for the poor); tzedakah is a Jewish justice-obligation; sewa is a Sikh pillar of practice, not optional; these traditions make helping the poor a divine command rather than personal choice.
Arguments against: Humanist and secular arguments (e.g. Peter Singer's utilitarian case) impose equal or greater duty based on reason alone; Oxfam and Shelter work alongside faith charities without religious motivation; the UK's welfare state redistributes wealth through taxation regardless of religion; a wealthy non-religious person who gives generously may fulfil a greater practical duty than a religious person who gives little.
Conclusion: should consider whether the source of obligation (divine command vs rational ethics) makes a genuine difference to the duty itself, and reach a clear personal stance.
Mastering: Sustained argument, both sides, named sources including charities and scripture, justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides with sources; conclusion reached.
Developing: One side stronger; limited sources.
Emerging: One-sided; few sources. [15 marks + 6 SPaG]

practice_questions.text: Give two principles of Catholic Social Teaching.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two: human dignity; the common good; solidarity; subsidiarity; care for creation; preferential option for the poor. Two marks maximum.

practice_questions.text: What does the term 'Catholic Social Teaching' mean?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: The body of Catholic teaching on the moral dimensions of economic, political and social life, rooted in the God-given dignity of every person and including principles such as the common good, solidarity and subsidiarity. Secure: Catholic teaching about justice, poverty and human dignity. Developing: The Church's teaching about helping others. Emerging: What Catholics believe about society.

practice_questions.text: Describe the work of CAFOD and explain how it is motivated by Catholic Social Teaching.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Accurate description of CAFOD (Catholic Agency for Overseas Development, official charity of Bishops' Conference of England and Wales, founded 1962, works in over 40 countries); explains what it does (emergency aid, development work, advocacy, Fast Days); links explicitly to CST — imago Dei means poverty is a moral injustice; mentions subsidiarity (working through local partners); or Gaudium et Spes 29. Secure: Accurate description with two features and one CST link. Developing: Some accurate content about CAFOD with basic CST mention. Emerging: Simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Explain the influence of the parable of the Good Samaritan on Catholic charity work in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains the parable (Luke 10:25–37 — Samaritan crosses boundaries to help a stranger); influence: models neighbour-love as crossing social/religious boundaries; motivates both CAFOD (reaching across global barriers) and SVP (personal presence with those in need, not just financial help); connects to Matthew 25:31–46 (serving Christ in the poor). Secure: Two developed points of influence. Developing: One developed point. Emerging: Simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Catholic belief in imago Dei shapes Catholic attitudes towards other religions. Refer to scripture or Church teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed ways with sources. Way 1: Imago Dei means every person — regardless of religion — has inherent dignity and deserves respect; this grounds inter-faith dialogue; Nostra Aetate (1965) acknowledged truth and goodness in other religions (Buddhism, Hinduism, Islam, Judaism). Way 2: Working with people of other faiths for the common good is itself an expression of love for God's image in the neighbour; the SVP and CAFOD work alongside non-Catholic partners. Each way with source and interpretation. Secure: Two ways with one source. Developing: One developed way. Emerging: Simple statement.

practice_questions.text: 'Giving to charity is more important than working for structural change in society.' Evaluate this statement from a Catholic perspective, considering more than one point of view.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: Immediate charity relieves urgent suffering — SVP visiting the housebound, CAFOD delivering emergency aid. The corporal works of mercy (Matthew 25:31–46) focus on concrete acts of kindness. Jesus' parable of the Good Samaritan shows direct personal help. Faith without works is dead (James 2:17). Arguments against: Catholic Social Teaching distinguishes between charity (addressing symptoms) and justice (addressing causes). Gaudium et Spes 29 and 78 call for transformation of social structures that violate human dignity. CAFOD campaigns for systemic change (debt relief, fair trade) alongside aid. Giving charity without challenging unjust structures can perpetuate the problem. Structural sin — the concept that unjust systems are themselves sinful — demands structural solutions. Non-religious view: Humanists would agree that systemic injustice must be addressed but might question whether religious motivation changes the nature of the action. Conclusion: A strong answer will argue that Catholic teaching holds both in tension — immediate charity is essential, but justice demands structural change. Mastering: Sustained two-sided argument, sources interpreted, clear conclusion. Secure: Two sides, one source. Developing: One side. Emerging: Simple view.

practice_questions.text: Give two features of a non-conformist Christian church.
practice_questions.marks: One mark per accurate feature, up to two. Examples: places greater emphasis on the Bible; more flexible worship style; no bishop or Pope; includes Baptist, Methodist and Pentecostal traditions. Mastering: two precise features using correct terminology. Emerging: one vague point.

practice_questions.text: What does 'agapé' mean in Christian ethics?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: agapé is unconditional, selfless love — the highest form of Christian love, identified with God's own love for humanity; the situational ethics approach uses it as the only absolute moral rule. Secure: accurate one-sentence definition. Emerging: 'love' without further explanation.

practice_questions.text: Describe Christian teaching about forgiveness.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5): detailed description including Matthew 18:21-22 (seventy-seven times), the Lord's Prayer link between receiving and giving forgiveness, Luke 23:34 (Jesus praying for forgiveness on the cross), and significance for Christian moral life. Secure (3-4): clear account of key teaching with some significance. Developing (2): basic reference to forgiving others. Emerging (1): simple statement that Christians forgive.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Christian teachings about the importance of love.
Refer to a source of Christian teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7-8): two well-developed beliefs, each with scripture and explanation of significance. Examples: (1) Love of neighbour is the second greatest commandment (Luke 10:25-37); the Parable of the Good Samaritan shows that this love must cross every boundary — race, religion, class — and motivates Christians to serve the poor and vulnerable. (2) Jesus gave a new commandment to love one another as he loved his disciples (John 13:34-35); this self-giving love is the distinguishing mark of Christian community and shapes how churches support their members. Secure (5-6): two beliefs developed with some source use. Developing (3-4): one strong point or two weak ones. Emerging (1-2): simple statements.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which the local church serves its community.
Refer to a source of Christian teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7-8): two well-developed ways, linked to scripture. Examples: (1) Spiritual function — the local church provides communal worship, prayer and the sacraments; Jesus taught that wherever two or three gather in his name, he is present (Matthew 18:20), making the gathered community itself a place of encounter with God. (2) Social justice function — churches run food banks, debt advice and support groups; Christian charities such as the Salvation Army extend this work nationally, motivated by Jesus' teaching about treasures in heaven (Matthew 6:19-21) and care for the neighbour (Luke 10). Secure (5-6): two ways with development. Developing (3-4): one developed way. Emerging (1-2): vague description.

practice_questions.text: 'Situational ethics is a better guide for Christians than divine command ethics.' Evaluate this statement, considering more than one point of view.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: situational ethics allows Christians to respond flexibly to complex modern situations not covered in the Bible; it prioritises love (agapé), which Jesus identified as the greatest commandment (Luke 10); it avoids the rigidity that can lead to harmful outcomes when rules are applied without compassion. Arguments against: divine command ethics provides clear, absolute moral rules that prevent subjective rationalisation; the Bible gives authoritative commands that Christians believe come from God; without fixed rules moral relativism can be used to justify almost any action; the Ten Commandments and Jesus' teachings provide firm guidance for most moral decisions. Conclusion: students should reach a justified personal view, weighing flexibility against moral clarity. Mastering (13-15): sustained argument, scripture integrated, clear conclusion. Secure (9-12): two sides with some source use. Developing (5-8): one-sided. Emerging (1-4): descriptive only.

practice_questions.text: Give two features of a Catholic church building and explain what each is used for.
practice_questions.marks: One mark per accurate feature with brief explanation, up to two marks. Examples: altar — used for the celebration of the Eucharist; font — used for baptism, usually near the entrance; lectern — where scripture is read aloud during the Mass; confessional — where the Sacrament of Reconciliation takes place. Mastering: two precise features with clear explanations. Emerging: one feature without explanation.

practice_questions.text: What does 'Advent' mean in the Catholic liturgical year?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Advent is the four-week season before Christmas — from the Latin word for 'coming' — in which Catholics prepare spiritually for the celebration of the Incarnation and look forward to Christ's promised return; it is marked by reflection, prayer and penance. Secure: accurate one-sentence definition. Emerging: 'the time before Christmas' without theological explanation.

practice_questions.text: Describe Catholic observances during Holy Week.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5): detailed description including Palm Sunday (entry into Jerusalem), Maundy Thursday (last supper, institution of the Eucharist, foot-washing), Good Friday (no Mass, Liturgy of the Word, Veneration of the Cross, Stations of the Cross), Holy Saturday (Easter Vigil — Paschal candle, baptism of converts, proclamation of Resurrection). Secure (3-4): clear account of main days with some significance. Developing (2): basic reference to Good Friday and Easter. Emerging (1): simple statement that Catholics remember Jesus' death.

practice_questions.text:
Explain how two seasons of the liturgical year influence Catholic belief and practice.
Refer to a source of Catholic teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7-8): two well-developed seasons, each with Catholic teaching reference. Examples: (1) Lent (forty days of fasting, prayer and penance) influences Catholics to examine their conscience, increase charitable giving and attend the Sacrament of Reconciliation; the forty days recall Jesus' time in the wilderness; the ashes on Ash Wednesday are a public sign of mortality and repentance, shaping Catholic identity. (2) Easter (CCC 1163) is the most important feast, celebrating the Resurrection and the promise of eternal life; the Easter Vigil (Paschal candle, adult baptisms, proclamation of Resurrection) makes this theology experientially present; it motivates Catholics' hope and sustains their faith through suffering. Secure (5-6): two seasons with development. Developing (3-4): one developed or two undeveloped. Emerging (1-2): simple statements.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two contrasting views about whether Catholics should go on pilgrimage.
Refer to sources of Christian teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7-8): two contrasting views well-developed with teaching references. Examples: (1) Pilgrimage deepens faith by taking Catholics physically to sacred places associated with Christ or the saints; Lourdes is associated with Marian apparitions and healing; the Catechism teaches that the Church's sacred places are points of encounter with the Mystery of Christ; pilgrimage also builds community among believers. (2) Some Christians argue that pilgrimage is unnecessary — Jesus taught that God is present wherever two or three gather (Matthew 18:20), not only at special sites; God is omnipresent and can be encountered in the local parish, in prayer, or in service to the poor; the cost and effort of pilgrimage might be better spent serving those in need. Secure (5-6): two contrasting views with development. Developing (3-4): one view. Emerging (1-2): simple statements.

practice_questions.text:
'Easter is more important than Christmas for Catholics.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
- refer to Catholic teaching
- give reasoned arguments to support this statement
- give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
- reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: the Catechism (CCC 1163) calls the liturgical year the unfolding of the Mystery of Christ, and Easter is at its heart; the Resurrection (John 20:1-21) is the event that conquers death and makes eternal life possible — without it, Paul argues, faith is pointless (1 Corinthians 15:14); the Easter Vigil is the most solemn liturgy of the year; Pentecost (following Easter) gave birth to the Church; the fifty days of Easter are longer than the Christmas season. Arguments against: Christmas celebrates the Incarnation — God becoming human — which is the foundational event that makes the crucifixion and Resurrection possible; without the Incarnation there would be nothing to celebrate at Easter; Christmas is arguably more culturally visible and may have greater influence on the wider population; Epiphany (the revelation to the Magi) emphasises the universal significance of Christ's coming. Conclusion: justified personal view, noting most Catholic theologians regard Easter as liturgically primary. Mastering (13-15): sustained argument, precise sources, clear conclusion. Secure (9-12): two sides. Developing (5-8): one-sided. Emerging (1-4): descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Give two sections of the Tenakh.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: Torah, Nevi'im (Prophets), Ketuvim (Writings).

practice_questions.text: What is the Talmud?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A vast collection of rabbinic debate and legal commentary on the Torah, compiled from the Mishnah (oral law) and Gemara (commentary), used to guide Jewish practice in all areas of life. Developing: A Jewish holy book with laws and rules.

practice_questions.text: Describe the brit milah ceremony and explain its significance for Jewish identity.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Describes the ceremony (eighth day, performed by the mohel, sandek holds the baby, father present) and explains significance (fulfils the Abrahamic Covenant, Genesis 17:11-14; physically marks the child as part of the covenant people; ties the individual to thousands of years of Jewish tradition). Secure: Accurate description with one clear reason for significance. Developing: Partial description, little explanation of significance. Emerging: Vague reference to circumcision as a Jewish practice.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the Abrahamic Covenant continues to influence Jewish life and identity today.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Genesis 12:1-3 and 17:6-8 cited; links to brit milah as physical sign; influence on Jewish sense of vocation ('chosen' = responsible); role of the covenant in diaspora Jewish identity and connection to Israel. Secure: Identifies the covenant and links it to one or two modern practices or beliefs. Developing: Describes the covenant without connecting to present-day influence. Emerging: Vague mention of Abraham and the Jewish people.

practice_questions.text: Explain two Jewish beliefs about the importance of the Torah, using sources of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed beliefs each with a named source. e.g. (1) Orthodox: Torah is the direct word of G-d, making every commandment binding; (2) Reform: Torah is divinely inspired but must be interpreted in light of modern ethics — both linked to Talmudic tradition or specific verses. Secure: Two beliefs with at least one source cited and interpreted. Developing: Two beliefs stated but not developed; sources absent. Emerging: One belief only.

practice_questions.text: 'The bar/bat mitzvah ceremony is the most important moment in a Jewish person's life.' Evaluate this statement, referring to Jewish teachings and non-religious perspectives.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Structured argument. Agree: marks full entry into religious adulthood, first public Torah reading, lifelong responsibility for mitzvot begins — deeply significant religiously. Disagree: brit milah (physical covenant sign from birth) and marriage might be equally important; some liberal Jews question gender distinctions; for non-practising Jews the ceremony may be cultural rather than spiritual. Non-religious view: secular transitions (e.g. turning 18) are more legally meaningful; the ceremony carries cultural rather than spiritual weight. Clear justified conclusion. Secure: Both sides with at least two sources; conclusion present. Developing: One-sided or superficial. Emerging: Simple assertion.

practice_questions.text: Give two reasons why Catholics use statues and sculptures in worship.
practice_questions.marks: Award one mark for each correct reason, up to two marks. Acceptable answers include: statues help believers focus their prayers / they serve as visual reminders of the holiness of Christ, Mary or a saint / they are used as a focus for contemplative prayer / the Church affirmed their use at the Council of Trent / Catholics venerate the person depicted, not the object itself.

practice_questions.text: What is the Pietà?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A marble sculpture by Michelangelo (completed c.1499) housed in St Peter's Basilica, Rome, depicting the Virgin Mary cradling the body of the crucified Christ; used as a focus for Catholic devotion and meditation on the Incarnation and Passion.

practice_questions.text: Describe how the Rosary is used in Catholic devotion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A detailed account that includes: the structure of the Rosary (beads, sequence of prayers including Hail Marys and Our Fathers), the four sets of Mysteries (Joyful, Luminous, Sorrowful, Glorious), the contemplative purpose (meditating on key Gospel events while reciting prayers), the Sorrowful Mysteries as a meditation on Christ's Passion, and the connection to Marian devotion and the Incarnation.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the Lourdes pilgrimage influences the lives of Catholic believers.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A developed explanation covering: Catholics travel to Lourdes seeking physical or spiritual healing, participate in communal worship (Mass, candlelit processions), bathe in or drink the spring water as an act of faith, and find community with other sick or suffering believers. The pilgrimage reinforces belief in the intercessory power of Mary and the physical reality of God's grace. British Catholic organisations including diocesan groups and hospital chaplaincies run annual pilgrimages, making it a communal expression of faith across the whole Church.
Secure: Two or more clear influences explained with some theological grounding.
Developing: One influence described but not well developed.
Emerging: A brief mention without explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Catholic beliefs about the significance of the Sorrowful Mysteries of the Rosary.
Refer to a source of Catholic teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two fully developed beliefs, each linked to a source of authority. Belief 1 might be that the Sorrowful Mysteries (the Agony in the Garden, Scourging, Crowning with Thorns, Carrying of the Cross, Crucifixion) allow Catholics to meditate on Christ's redemptive suffering — connected to the Catholic doctrine that suffering united with Christ's Passion has salvific meaning (Catechism 1521). Belief 2 might be that the Rosary as a whole is a 'Gospel prayer' (Pope Paul VI, Marialis Cultus, 1974) drawing directly from scripture, making Marian devotion an act of scriptural contemplation rather than superstition.
Secure: Two beliefs clearly explained, each with a relevant source of authority named.
Developing: One belief explained well; the second belief is superficial or lacks a source.
Emerging: One brief point without development or source.

practice_questions.text:
'Statues and sculptures are more likely to distract Catholics from genuine worship than to help them.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Catholic teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Some Protestant reformers argued that images in churches lead believers to focus on the object rather than God, risking idolatry (a concern reflected in the Reformation's iconoclasm).
• A secular or humanist critic might argue that emotional attachment to physical objects is psychologically understandable but theologically confused — the statue does not actually connect the believer to the divine.
• Even within Catholicism, popular piety can drift into superstition if believers think the statue itself has power rather than the person it represents.

Arguments against:
• The Catholic Church explicitly teaches (CCC 2132) that veneration of sacred images is legitimate: Catholics honour the prototype, not the image. The Council of Trent affirmed the proper use of sacred images.
• Statues such as the Pieta mediate theological content visually — the image of Mary holding Christ's body communicates the Incarnation, Passion and redemption in a way that transcends literacy or formal theological education.
• Lourdes pilgrimage, Rosary and Marian shrines have demonstrably deepened the faith of millions of Catholics, offering communal encounters with God that abstract doctrine alone cannot provide.
• Pope Paul VI and Pope John Paul II explicitly endorsed popular piety, including the Rosary, as authentic expressions of Catholic faith.

Conclusion: A justified conclusion should weigh the risk of superstition against the Church's affirmation of sacred images, and acknowledge that the distinction between veneration and worship is the Catholic answer to the critique.

Mastering: Sophisticated argument on both sides with named sources and a clear justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides developed with some sources and a conclusion.
Developing: One-sided or conclusion missing.
Emerging: Simple statements without reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Give two examples of Christian denominations or groups that hold contrasting views on same-sex relationships.

[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how the Catholic Church teaches believers to respond to same-sex attraction and same-sex relationships.
practice_questions.marks:

Developing: Description of one element with limited reasoning.
Emerging: Simple statement that the Catholic Church is against same-sex relationships with no further development. [5 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how two contrasting religious attitudes towards same-sex relationships are shaped by different interpretations of scripture.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two well-developed contrasting views (e.g. traditionalist Christian reading of Leviticus 20:13 vs progressive contextual reading; Orthodox Jewish vs Reform Jewish use of Leviticus 18:22) each with a named scripture reference, explanation of what the text says, and explanation of how/why the two groups interpret it differently.
Secure: Two contrasting views each linked to a named source with some explanation of the interpretive difference.
Developing: Two views identified but one is more developed; limited use of sources.
Emerging: One view described with minimal use of scripture. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two beliefs that lead some Muslims to oppose same-sex marriage.
Refer to a source of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct beliefs (e.g. marriage is understood as a covenant between a man and woman ordained by God; sexual activity outside this is prohibited by reference to Qur'an 7:80-81; human nature and fitra are created with a specific design) each developed with explanation of what the belief means and how it leads to opposition to same-sex marriage, with at least one Qur'anic reference interpreted.

practice_questions.text:
'Religious communities should fully accept same-sex relationships.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to religious teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support: Quakers argue the divine light is present in every person regardless of orientation; Reform Judaism grounds acceptance in kavod ha-beriyot (human dignity) and neighbour-love; Humanists appeal to consent and wellbeing as the only morally relevant criteria; Galatians 3:28 ('neither male nor female in Christ') used by progressive Christians to support inclusion; the Marriage Act has given legal recognition showing society accepts these relationships.
Arguments against: Catholic Catechism 2357-2359 teaches same-sex sexual activity is contrary to natural law; Leviticus 20:13 and 1 Timothy 1:8-10 cited by traditionalists; Islamic teaching from Qur'an 7:80-81 sees such relationships as contrary to divine order; Sikh Rehat Maryada defines marriage as between a man and a woman; Buddhist Third Precept interpreted by some as implying the same.
Conclusion: should weigh whether religious teachings are best understood as timeless commands or as contextual guidance, and take a clear personal stance.
Mastering: Balanced, sustained argument with multiple named sources and a justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides developed with sources; conclusion reached.
Developing: One side stronger; limited sources.
Emerging: Simple points, one-sided. [15 marks. Spelling, punctuation and grammar carry extra marks on specified extended-writing questions.]

practice_questions.text: Give two sacraments that belong to the category of Sacraments of Initiation.

practice_questions.text: What does 'transubstantiation' mean in Catholic teaching?

practice_questions.text: Explain how Evangelii Gaudium has influenced the way Catholics approach mission in Britain today.

practice_questions.text: 'Receiving the sacraments is more important for a Catholic than evangelising.' Evaluate this statement, referring to Catholic teachings and non-religious perspectives.

practice_questions.text: Give two reasons why Catholics pray for those who have died.
practice_questions.marks: Award one mark for each correct reason, up to two. practice_questions.text: What does the Catholic Church mean by 'formulaic prayer'?
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Prayer using fixed texts handed down by the Church, such as the Lord's Prayer, the Hail Mary or the Rosary; said using the same words each time; connects the individual to the tradition of the whole Church.

Emerging: A type of Catholic prayer.

practice_questions.text: Describe how British Catholic communities pray for the dead.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A detailed description covering: Masses offered for deceased relatives on anniversaries or All Souls' Day (2 November); the book of the dead in parish churches during November listing names of the recently deceased; prayers for the dead included in every Mass within the Eucharistic Prayer; lighting candles before statues as acts of popular piety; the theological basis (purgatory, Communion of Saints) underlying all these practices.
Secure: Two or more practices described with some theological connection.
Developing: One practice described without theological grounding.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the Lord's Prayer (Matthew 6:9–13) influences Catholic worship and prayer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A developed explanation covering: the Lord's Prayer is the model for all Christian prayer (Catechism calls it 'the summary of the whole gospel'); it structures prayer around adoration ('hallowed be your name'), petition ('give us today our daily bread'), forgiveness ('forgive us our sins') and protection ('deliver us from evil'); it is prayed at every Mass, at baptisms and funerals, and at the graveside committal; it unites all Catholics in a common language of prayer regardless of language or culture.
Secure: Two or more influences explained with scriptural or Catechism reference.
Developing: One influence without depth.
Emerging: Brief mention of the prayer.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Catholic beliefs about the Communion of Saints.
Refer to a source of Catholic teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two fully developed beliefs with sources. Belief 1 might be that the Communion of Saints (CCC 946–962) teaches that all who are united to Christ — the living, the souls in purgatory, and the saints in heaven — form one community; death does not break the bonds of charity. Belief 2 might be that the saints in heaven intercede for the living, just as Jesus himself intercedes (Romans 8:34), and Mary's intercession is specially valued ('pray for us sinners, now and at the hour of our death' — Hail Mary); this is why Catholics pray to and through the saints.
Secure: Two beliefs explained with sources.
Developing: One belief well explained, second superficial.
Emerging: One brief point.

practice_questions.text:
'Praying for the dead is meaningless because death ends personal existence.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to Catholic teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• A Humanist or secular view holds that consciousness ends at death — there is no soul to be assisted, no purgatory to be shortened, and no God to receive the prayer.
• From a purely psychological perspective, prayer for the dead benefits the bereaved (it helps them grieve and stay connected to the memory of the deceased) but has no effect on the person who has died.
• Some Protestants reject the doctrine of purgatory and therefore reject prayers for the dead as unscriptural and potentially misleading.

Arguments against:
• The Catholic Church teaches that purgatory is a real state (CCC 1030–1032) and that prayers and Masses for the dead genuinely assist souls in their purification before heaven.
• The Communion of Saints (CCC 946–962) teaches that love and prayer transcend death: the living and the dead are united in one community in Christ.
• Offering Mass for the dead applies the merits of Christ's sacrifice — the Eucharist makes present the once-for-all sacrifice of Calvary — to the needs of the soul in purgatory.
• Prayer for the dead has been part of the Church's practice since at least the second century (2 Maccabees 12:46 is cited in Catholic tradition), suggesting it is rooted in authentic faith.

Conclusion: A justified conclusion should weigh the secular argument (death as the end of consciousness) against the Catholic theological case (purgatory, Communion of Saints, Mass as sacrifice) and reach a clear personal stance.

Mastering: Sophisticated argument with named sources and justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides with some sources and a conclusion.
Developing: One-sided or conclusion missing.
Emerging: Simple statements without reasoning.

Secure: Two clear features with some explanation of belief-link.
Developing: One or two features described, belief connection weak.
Emerging: Simple statement only.

Secure: Two points linking Humanist practice to Humanist belief.
Developing: One point developed.

Explain two contrasting religious views on the correct way to treat a dead body.
Refer to sources of authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two contrasting practices (e.g. Islamic burial — kafan, qiblah, speed — rooted in belief in resurrection of the body and akhirah (Qur'an 46:33); Buddhist cremation — reflecting anicca, the example of the Buddha, transfer of merit to the deceased) each developed with a source of authority and explanation of why the practice flows from the belief.
Secure: Two contrasting views, one source, some development.
Developing: Two practices described without full belief-link.
Emerging: One practice only.

practice_questions.text:
'Religious funeral rites are more meaningful than Humanist funerals.'
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• refer to religious teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Catholic funerals connect the bereaved to centuries of tradition, scripture (John 11:25) and the community of the Church (CCC 1684-1690) — this communal dimension adds significance beyond the individual.
• Religious funerals affirm resurrection or rebirth, giving mourners hope that death is not the final word.
• Islamic, Jewish and Sikh funeral rites are precise and purposeful — each element (kafan, shiva, Kirtan Sohila) carries theological weight that a purely secular ceremony may lack.
Arguments against:
• Humanist funerals are personally tailored to the individual's life, values and character — supporters argue this is more genuinely meaningful than following a set liturgy.
• For the non-religious bereaved, a religious funeral may feel alien or dishonest — a Humanist ceremony may better reflect the reality of the person's life and beliefs.
• The purpose of a funeral is to comfort the bereaved and honour the dead — Humanist ceremonies achieve this without requiring shared theological commitments.
Conclusion: Justified personal judgement.
Mastering: Two sides sustained, multiple religious traditions referenced, Humanist view included, clear justified conclusion that weighs the evidence.
Secure: Both sides, one source, conclusion present.
Developing: One side stronger.
Emerging: One-sided, no conclusion.

practice_questions.marks: Mastering: A ram's horn blown as a musical instrument during Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, whose sound calls Jews to repentance and self-examination before G-d. Developing: A horn blown at Jewish festivals.

Secure: Two clear ways Pesach connects Jews to history with some explanation. Developing: One way described without full explanation. Emerging: Vague reference to Passover celebrating freedom.

practice_questions.text: Explain two Jewish beliefs about repentance, using sources of wisdom and authority.

Secure: Two beliefs with at least one source. Developing: Two beliefs stated briefly; sources absent. Emerging: One belief only.

practice_questions.text: 'Yom Kippur is more important for Jewish identity than Pesach.' Evaluate this statement, referring to Jewish teachings and non-religious perspectives.

Agree: Yom Kippur is the holiest day; it culminates the Days of Awe; Kol Nidre draws even secular Jews; atonement is central to the Jewish relationship with G-d. Mastering: Two genuinely contrasting views (e.g. Christian unconditional forgiveness from Matthew 18:21–22 vs. Jewish teshuvah requiring genuine repentance before forgiveness is due; or Buddhist metta extending forgiveness universally vs. Islamic allowance for proportionate retaliation in Qur'an 42:40). Both views developed and contrast clearly drawn.

Emerging: One view or very limited development. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Religious believers can explain why evil and suffering exist.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to religious teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• The Augustinian theodicy (Genesis 3 / free-will defence) provides a coherent explanation that evil resulted from human choice, not God's design.
• Buddhist teaching on the Three Poisons (lobha, dosa, moha) explains the origin of suffering precisely and coherently.
• Hindu karma provides a complete causal account of why individuals suffer differently.

Arguments against:
• Natural evil (earthquakes, disease) is not explained by free will.
• The Holocaust challenges whether theodicy is adequate for extreme suffering.
• Humanists / Richard Dawkins argue that suffering is better explained by evolution than theology, and that no theodicy truly resolves the logical problem of evil.

Mastering: Sophisticated, balanced evaluation; multiple traditions engaged; Humanist view included; clear justified personal conclusion.
Secure: Two developed viewpoints; conclusion present.
Developing: Some argument, limited balance or weak conclusion.
Emerging: One-sided or minimal. [15 marks + SPaG 5%]

practice_questions.text: Give two ways in which religious believers act to promote human rights.

Each reason explained with a named source and linked explicitly to racial prejudice. Secure: Two reasons with sources; adequate development. Developing: One reason explained; the second underdeveloped. Emerging: General anti-racism statements without religious grounding.

Argues against (religious institutions have also violated rights: historical examples; secular organisations like Amnesty International defend rights independently of religion; Humanists UK argues rights are stronger when grounded in universal reason, not contested doctrine). Weighs both sides. Clear justified personal conclusion. Secure: Both sides with named sources; conclusion reached. Developing: One-sided with a brief nod to the other view. Emerging: Simple personal opinion.

practice_questions.text: What does the term 'papal infallibility' mean?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: The teaching that the Pope cannot err when defining, with full formal authority (ex cathedra), a matter of faith or morals for the universal Church. Secure: The Pope is infallible when formally teaching on faith or morals. Developing: The Pope is always right. Emerging: The Pope has authority.

practice_questions.text: Describe the Catholic understanding of the Church as the 'Body of Christ'.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Detailed description of the Pauline image — Christ as head, believers as members, the Church as a living unity with diverse parts serving one purpose; reference to how this shapes Catholic self-understanding, including the role of baptism in incorporating a person into the Body. Secure: Clear description with two or more features, including one explained significance. Developing: Some relevant content with basic description. Emerging: Simple point such as 'the Church is like a body'.

practice_questions.text:
Explain how the teaching on Mary as Theotokos influences Catholic belief and practice.
Refer to a source of authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains that Theotokos (Council of Ephesus, 431) affirms Jesus is truly divine; this underpins Marian devotion — if Mary bore God, she deserves special honour; influences practice such as Marian shrines, the rosary, intercessionary prayer. Reference to a source (e.g. CCC, Hail Mary prayer, Matthew 1:18–25 or Luke 1:26–35) and its interpretation. Secure: Two developed points with one source. Developing: One developed point. Emerging: Simple statement.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Catholic beliefs about the authority of the Pope.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Catholic belief and teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed beliefs, each with a source and interpretation. Belief 1: The Pope is St Peter's successor — Jesus's words in Matthew 16:18 ('on this rock I will build my church') established Peter as the foundation; the Pope inherits this authority through apostolic succession. Belief 2: Papal infallibility — when the Pope speaks ex cathedra on faith or morals, he is protected from error; this was defined at Vatican I (1870) and used for the Assumption (1950). Each belief explains the significance and links the source to the doctrine. Secure: Two beliefs each with a source. Developing: One fully developed belief or two underdeveloped. Emerging: Simple statements.

practice_questions.text:
'Venerating Mary is no different from worshipping God.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to Catholic teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: Some argue Marian devotion in practice looks like worship — Catholics pray to her, build shrines, make pilgrimages and credit her with miracles. If she intercedes for believers, she seems to occupy a divine role. The distinction between latria and hyperdulia may seem academic when a believer prays the Hail Mary daily. Arguments against: Catholic theology formally distinguishes veneration (hyperdulia — special honour to Mary) from worship (latria — due only to God). Mary is honoured because of her relationship to Christ, not because she is God. Intercessionary prayer asks Mary to pray for believers — it is directed through her to God. The Catechism is explicit: only God is worshipped. Non-religious view: Humanists may argue that prayer to any supernatural being is indistinguishable in practice; the theological distinction is meaningful only within the framework of belief. Conclusion: A strong answer will judge whether the distinction holds up in practice, not just in theory — candidates may argue the doctrinal distinction is clear and real, or that popular practice sometimes blurs it. Mastering: Sustained two-sided argument, sources, named theological distinction, justified conclusion. Secure: Two sides, one source. Developing: One side with some development. Emerging: Simple one-sided view.

practice_questions.text: Give two different Christian attitudes towards women serving as priests or ministers.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for: The Catholic Church reserves ordination to men citing apostolic tradition / The Church of England and Church in Wales ordain women as priests and bishops. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: What does the term 'ordination' mean in a religious context?
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for: the rite or ceremony by which a person is set apart or consecrated as a minister, priest, or religious leader [1 mark for a basic definition; 2 marks for a clear definition with reference to formal religious appointment or consecration]. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe Jewish attitudes towards the roles of women and men in worship and religious authority.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Detailed description that distinguishes Orthodox from Reform Judaism — Orthodox: women exempt from time-bound commandments, separate seating, no female rabbis; Reform: women ordained as rabbis since the 1970s, mixed seating, full participation — with explanation of the reasons (halakha vs reinterpretation in light of human equality).
Secure: Two contrasting positions described with some explanation.
Developing: One position described with limited development.
Emerging: Simple statement that Jews hold different views. [5 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two beliefs that support the view that women and men should have equal roles in religious worship.
Refer to sources of wisdom and authority from at least two different traditions in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct beliefs from different traditions, each with a named source and interpretation explaining why the belief leads to equal roles. E.g. Galatians 3:27-29 (in Christ no male or female — all one in him); Guru Granth Sahib ang 473 (from woman all are born — affirming women's spiritual status); Qur'an 40:40 (equal spiritual accountability for all believers). Each belief developed with explanation.
Secure: Two beliefs each with a named source; adequate explanation.
Developing: Two beliefs; one developed with a source.
Emerging: One belief; limited development. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain two contrasting Islamic views on the roles of women and men in worship and religious authority.
Refer to sources of wisdom and authority in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Traditional view — women do not lead mixed Friday prayers; Qur'an 2:228 ('men have a degree over them') has been used to support this; contemporary view — some scholars argue restrictions were culturally conditioned and that Qur'an 4:1 (common origin) and 40:40 (equal accountability) point to full spiritual equality. Both views developed with named sources and explained.
Secure: Two contrasting views each with a source; clear explanation of the difference.
Developing: Two views, limited source use.
Emerging: One view described. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Religious traditions should give men and women completely equal roles in worship and leadership.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should: refer to religious teaching; give reasoned arguments to support this statement; give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support: Galatians 3:27-29 points to equality in Christ; Guru Granth Sahib ang 473 affirms women's spiritual status; Reform Judaism ordains women rabbis on the basis of human equality; Humanists point to the Equality Act 2010; Qur'an 40:40 and 4:1 affirm equal spiritual standing; many denominations (Church of England, Quakers, Reform synagogues) have moved to equal roles and thrive.
Arguments against: Catholic Church teaches priestly ordination is restricted to men (Catechism 1577) by apostolic tradition; 1 Timothy 2:11-12 is read by some as restricting women's teaching authority; Theravada tradition has historically maintained gendered ordination structures; complementarian view holds men and women have different but equally valued roles; religious organisations have some Equality Act exemptions to protect this.
Conclusion: should weigh whether human dignity requires identical roles or merely equal value, and reach a clear, justified personal stance.
Mastering: Sustained balanced argument, multiple named sources, clear justified conclusion.
Secure: Both sides with sources; conclusion reached.
Developing: One side stronger; limited sources.
Emerging: One-sided; few sources. [15 marks. Spelling, punctuation and grammar carry extra marks on specified extended-writing questions.]

practice_questions.text: Give two reasons why a Christian might go on a pilgrimage.
practice_questions.marks: One mark per accurate reason, up to two. Examples: to seek healing; to deepen faith; to pray in a sacred place; to give thanks; to feel closer to the events of Jesus' life. Mastering: two precise reasons linked to Christian belief. Emerging: one vague point.

practice_questions.text: What does 'sacrament' mean in Christianity?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: a sacrament is an outward, physical sign of an inward, spiritual grace — a sacred ritual believed to convey God's grace to the participant. Secure: accurate one-sentence definition. Emerging: 'a religious ceremony' without further explanation.

practice_questions.text: Describe Christian teaching about life after death.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5): detailed description including John 3:16 (eternal life through belief), John 14:1-4 (Jesus preparing a place), 1 Corinthians 15:20-22 (resurrection in Christ), Matthew 25:31-46 (judgement based on care for others), and heaven/hell. Secure (3-4): clear account with some scripture. Developing (2): basic mention of heaven or resurrection. Emerging (1): simple statement that Christians believe in life after death.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two Christian views on how the Bible should be interpreted.
Refer to a source of Christian teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7-8): two well-developed views, each with explanation of significance. Examples: (1) A literal approach holds that the Bible is accurate in every historical and scientific detail; this view is supported by 2 Timothy 3:16-17 (all scripture is God-breathed); believers holding this view accept the Genesis creation account as factual and see no contradiction between faith and the Bible's exact text. (2) A symbolic interpretation sees much of the Bible as conveying spiritual truth through metaphor and story; supporters argue the Bible's purpose is to reveal God, not to be a history textbook; Genesis on this reading teaches that God is Creator and humans are made in God's image, without requiring a literal six-day creation. Secure (5-6): two views with development. Developing (3-4): one view developed. Emerging (1-2): simple statements.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two contrasting views about the Eucharist.
Refer to sources of Christian teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7-8): two contrasting views well-developed with scripture. Examples: (1) Catholics believe in transubstantiation — the bread and wine actually become the body and blood of Christ; this is rooted in 1 Corinthians 11:23-26 where Jesus says 'this is my body'; the Eucharist is the central act of Catholic worship and is treated with great reverence. (2) Many Protestant Christians hold a memorial or symbolic view — the bread and wine represent Christ's body and blood but do not change their substance; the Eucharist is an act of remembrance proclaiming his death 'until he comes again'. Secure (5-6): two contrasting views with some source use. Developing (3-4): one view or two undeveloped points. Emerging (1-2): simple statements.

practice_questions.text: 'Going on a pilgrimage is the best way for a Christian to deepen their faith.' Evaluate this statement, considering more than one point of view.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: pilgrimage takes Christians physically to places where Jesus lived and died, making their faith feel more real and immediate; Lourdes and other shrines are associated with healing and spiritual transformation; the effort and sacrifice of the journey itself can deepen commitment; communal pilgrimage builds shared faith with other believers (Matthew 18:20 — where two or three gather). Arguments against: Jesus taught that private prayer in one's own room is equally valid (Matthew 6:6); the local church and Bible study are just as effective for deepening faith; pilgrimage can be expensive and inaccessible; many Christians develop deep faith through daily Bible reading, prayer and service without ever travelling to a sacred site; the Reformation tradition emphasises that God is present everywhere, not specially located at shrines. Conclusion: a justified personal view. Mastering (13-15): sustained argument, scripture integrated, clear conclusion. Secure (9-12): two sides with some source use. Developing (5-8): one-sided. Emerging (1-4): descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Give two examples of mendicant religious orders in the Catholic Church.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two: Franciscans; Dominicans; Carmelites. Two marks maximum.

practice_questions.text: What is meant by the term 'evangelical counsels'?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: The three vows of poverty, chastity and obedience taken by members of religious orders, described as 'evangelical' because they are drawn from the example and teaching of Christ in the Gospels. Secure: The three vows of poverty, chastity and obedience. Developing: Vows taken by monks and nuns. Emerging: Rules that religious follow.

practice_questions.text: Describe the meaning and significance of the Crucifix in Catholic Christianity.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Detailed description of what the Crucifix shows (Christ's body on the cross), why it differs from the bare Protestant cross (it emphasises the suffering and death of the Incarnate Son), where it is displayed and why (churches, homes — constant reminder of salvation through Christ's sacrifice). Reference to what it communicates theologically. Secure: Two features with one explained significance. Developing: One feature with basic description. Emerging: Simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Explain the influence of the vow of poverty on the life of a member of a religious order.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains poverty means giving up personal ownership; everything held in common; influence on daily life — no personal possessions, dependence on community; theological reason — following Christ who had nowhere to lay his head (Matthew 8:20); influence on attitude to wealth and service of the poor; challenge of the vow and how it is understood as freeing. Secure: Two developed points of influence. Developing: One developed point. Emerging: Simple statement.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which Catholic art or symbols express beliefs about Jesus Christ.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Catholic belief and teaching in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed ways, each with source and interpretation. Way 1: Michelangelo's Creation of Adam expresses imago Dei — humans are made in God's image (Genesis 1:26); the gap between God's and Adam's fingers shows life as a divine gift; the painting communicates the dignity of human life. Way 2: The Chi-Rho symbol declares Christ's identity as Lord — taken from the Greek letters of Christos; adopted by Emperor Constantine; used as a declaration of faith. Or the Crucifix — expresses the Incarnation (God truly suffered) and the means of salvation. Each way explained with theological significance and a source. Secure: Two ways with one source. Developing: One developed way. Emerging: Simple identification.

practice_questions.text:
'The Rosary is the most important form of Catholic prayer.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to Catholic teaching
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks: Arguments in support: The Rosary unites Marian devotion, Trinitarian prayer and scriptural meditation in one practice. Pope John Paul II called it a contemplation of the face of Christ through Mary's eyes. It is widely used by Catholics globally, can be prayed anywhere and is a deeply personal form of devotion. Arguments against: The Mass (Eucharist) is the 'source and summit' of Catholic life — it is a sacrament instituted by Christ himself. Liturgical prayer (the Divine Office) is the official prayer of the Church. Private meditation, lectio divina and personal prayer are also highly valued. Many Catholics do not pray the Rosary but have a rich prayer life. Non-religious view: From a Humanist perspective, no prayer form is meaningful, but the Rosary is noted as a powerful meditative practice with psychological benefits similar to other forms of structured meditation. Conclusion: A strong answer will weigh Marian devotion against sacramental and communal prayer; a personal stance taken and justified. Mastering: Sustained argument, two sides, sources, conclusion. Secure: Two sides, one source. Developing: One side developed. Emerging: Simple statement.
